articles.title: `npm config get` Knows Which Layer Won. It Just Won't Tell You.
articles.description: fluffydesk left a comment on my last piece about .npmrc layers, and it named the exact check I had...
articles.body_html:
fluffydesk left a comment on my last piece about .npmrc layers, and it named the exact check I had been skipping. I had shown that a repo's own .npmrc beats your user config: my user file says ignore-scripts=true, the repo says false, and the repo wins: the install hook runs. The check I recommended was npm config list, run inside the repo before installing, because it names the winning file.

fluffydesk asked about the check people actually run instead. npm config get ignore-scripts answers with the merged value from wherever you are standing: false inside the repo, true from home. Same command, two answers, and no mention that a vote happened. Worse, --location=user does not rescue it. The flag is accepted, and the command still returns false.

So I ran the comparison. Same setup as last time: user config true, project config false, a test package with an install hook that leaves a marker file when it runs. Thirteen commands, three locations, every answer recorded. The flag does nothing. That is the claim, and I know it sounds like a small thing, but a flag that is accepted and ignored is worse than a flag that errors, because it lets you walk away believing you asked one layer a question and got its answer.

Problem 1: the same command gives two answers, and neither says why

Inside the repo, npm config get ignore-scripts prints false. From home, the same command prints true. From the folder above the repo, true again. All three answers are the effective value for that spot, and all three are correct in the narrow sense. The install proves it: the hook ran in the repo and did not run in the clean folder. But none of them says which layer won. If you run the check from home and read true, you walk into the install believing hooks are off. They are not. The command answered the question you typed and hid the question you meant: who decided this?

That is the trap in its plainest form. The value is right and the understanding is wrong, and the understanding is the part that costs you.

Problem 2: --location=user is accepted, and then ignored

This is the one fluffydesk called, and they called it exactly. Inside the repo, npm config get ignore-scripts --location=user returns false. Not true, the user layer's value. false, the project-overridden value. The flag does not error, does not warn, does not print anything extra. It just takes your request to hear from the user layer and hands you the merged answer anyway.

I ran it from all three spots to be sure. Home: true. Run root: true. Inside the repo: false, with the flag on. The flag changes nothing about the value anywhere. If you believed --location=user was a way to interrogate one layer at a time, you were never interrogating anything. You were asking the same merged question with extra words attached.

A flag that errors is honest. A flag that is silently ignored is a trap with good manners.

Problem 3: --location=project outside a repo answers instead of refusing

The other direction is worse, because it invents an answer. From home, where no project config exists at all, npm config get ignore-scripts --location=project returns true, the user value, with no warning that there is no project layer to ask. From the run root, same thing: true, silence, no complaint.

Read that as a person would. You asked the project layer a question, and it answered. Except it did not. There is no project layer there. The command reached past the layer you named, took the next value down the chain, and handed it to you dressed as a project answer. If you are writing a check that runs in CI, in a directory you did not verify first, that silent fallback is the difference between "the repo has no override" and "I never actually looked at the repo".

Problem 4: only one command names the winner, and it is not the one with JSON

Plain npm config list, run from inside the repo, is the only command in the whole matrix that tells you which layer won. It prints the user value true stamped ; overridden by project, then names the winning file by its full path, ; "project" config from .../repo/.npmrc, and then the effective false. That stamp is the whole story in one line: a vote happened, here is who lost, here is the file that beat them.

npm config list --json shows "ignore-scripts": false and names no source file at all. So the machine-readable version is the one that drops the one fact you need, and the human-readable version is the one that keeps it. If your tooling parses the JSON, it gets the value and loses the provenance in the same breath.

And config list only tells the truth from inside the repo. From the parent folder, the project layer is invisible: true, user file named, no project section. Same command, same honesty, but the answer depends on where you stand, and standing in the wrong place is the easiest mistake in the whole chain.

Command Inside repo/ From home From outside Names the winner?
npm config get ignore-scripts false true true No
... --location=user false true true No
... --location=project false true true No
npm config list false true true Yes
npm config list --json false — — No

Every command took about 0.2 seconds. The check costs nothing. The wrong check costs a hook running on a machine you thought was protected.

Problem 5: the value was never wrong, which is why this keeps biting

Here is the part that keeps me from calling the whole thing broken. npm config get gets the effective value right every time. The install confirms it: hook ran in the repo at 00:14:01 UTC, no marker in the clean folder. If all you need is "what will the install do", get answers correctly from the right directory.

But "what will the install do" is not the question people are asking when they type get. They are asking "am I safe", and safety is a question about layers, not values. A true from home is not a promise about the repo. A false inside the repo is not an explanation of who set it. The command gives you the outcome and withholds the cause, and the cause is the thing you need when the outcome surprises you at 2 a.m. in a CI log.

So the rule I am keeping is narrow, and it is the same shape as the last piece: cd into the repo, then plain npm config list, not --json. Not because get lies. It does not. But because it answers the question you typed while the question you meant goes unasked. And if you ever catch yourself adding --location to make the answer more specific, stop. It is accepted, it changes nothing, and the silence afterwards is the command agreeing with a premise it never checked.

What check have you run that reported the loser without mentioning a vote happened? I would like to hear which command it was, and whether you found out from the output or from the hook running anyway.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: I Built MLBox: A Browser Workbench That Shows How LLM Tokenizers Really Work
articles.description: Hi, I'm Mohit Verma, a Class 10 student from Patna, India, learning machine learning by building...
articles.body_html:
Hi, I'm Mohit Verma, a Class 10 student from Patna, India, learning machine learning by building things. MLBox is my open-source project: a browser workbench for LLM tokenizers, training intuition, and API pricing. Four tools, one static page, zero dependencies — every number is measured in your own browser.

Live demo: https://mohittt-vermaa.github.io/mlbox/
Code: https://github.com/mohittt-vermaa/mlbox

What's inside

Tokenizer lens — Paste any text and watch 7 real LLM tokenizers cut it up, token by token: counts, cost per million characters, a language cost matrix, a boundary diff between any two tokenizers, and a shareable link that freezes the whole comparison.

Micro playground — A neural net with hand-written backprop training live on canvas. Watch gradient descent solve XOR.

No-GPU recipes — 12 curated ML projects that genuinely finish on a laptop or a free Colab session, each with its one gotcha spelled out.

LLM price bench — 13 current models from 5 providers, transcribed from each provider's own pricing page with source links, plus a workload calculator and a real-prompt cost estimator.

The number that motivated all of this

Paste "नमस्ते दुनिया" ("hello world" in Hindi, 13 characters) and the tokenizers disagree: GPT-4o's tokenizer needs 5 tokens, Llama 3.1 needs 9, GPT-3.5/4's cl100k needs 13. Same two words, nearly 3x the bill depending on which tokenizer sits in front. Token choice is a cost multiplier and a context-window multiplier, and almost nobody looks at it.

Verified, not approximate

The tokenizer engine re-implements both BPE families in about 550 lines of dependency-free JavaScript, and the test suite checks it token-for-token against the upstream Rust implementations: 218,877 tokens, exact match on all seven models. There is also an Android app and a Windows desktop build in the releases, and everything runs offline with no API key and no backend — your text never leaves your machine.

Why I built it

I kept reading claims about token costs from blog posts instead of measuring them. MLBox is my way of learning ML properly: build the tool, verify every number, and share it so the next student can measure things themselves.

If it helps you, a star on GitHub means a lot: https://github.com/mohittt-vermaa/mlbox

— Mohit Verma
All my work: https://mohittt-vermaa.github.io

articles.title: Five trigger WHEN clauses Postgres will reject
articles.description: Postgres will reject some trigger WHEN clauses, but only when the migration runs.  A few rules that...
articles.body_html:
Postgres will reject some trigger WHEN clauses, but only when the migration runs.

A few rules that catch people out:

  1. A statement-level trigger can't read OLD or NEW in its WHEN. There's no single row to compare.
  2. An INSERT trigger can't read OLD. There is no old row.
  3. A DELETE trigger can't read NEW. There is no new row.
  4. An INSTEAD OF trigger on a view can't have a WHEN at all.
  5. A WHEN can't contain a subquery.

If you write triggers by hand in a custom migration, you find these out at deploy time.

In drizzle-pg-extras, my open-source package for declaring Postgres triggers, functions, comments and extensions next to a Drizzle schema, pgTrigger checks these when you declare the trigger, so generate fails before a bad migration is written:

export const touchUsers = pgTrigger("users_set_updated_at", {
  table: users,
  timing: "before",
  events: ["update"],
  columns: [users.email], // UPDATE OF
  when: ({ OLD, NEW }) => sql`${OLD.email} IS DISTINCT FROM ${NEW.email}`,
  function: setUpdatedAt,
});

It's a text scan, not a SQL parser, so Postgres still reports anything else when the migration runs. The README now spells out exactly what's checked and what isn't (0.6.1, on npm).

GitHub: https://github.com/Robertpaschal/drizzle-pg-extras
npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/drizzle-pg-extras

articles.title: Browser Autofill Testing: Follow the Filled Form Into the Saved SaaS Record
articles.description: Browser autofill testing should follow the values all the way into the saved product record. Start...
articles.body_html:
Browser autofill testing should follow the values all the way into the saved product record. Start with safe test details, choose a browser suggestion, inspect every field it fills, correct one value, submit the form, and reopen the result. A form that looks complete may still behave differently from one filled by typing.

For a founder building in public, that is a useful peer-testing request. It gives another developer a specific task to try in a known environment. The public update can show the observed mismatch and recovery without exposing the tester's real address, contact list or browser profile.

Define the record the form is meant to create

Use a fictional SaaS contact manager as an example. Its new-contact form asks for a person's name, organization, email and postal address. The intended result is one contact record containing the reviewed values. Creating the record must not send an invitation or start a sales email in this exercise.

Prepare a disposable test workspace and confirm those boundaries before asking a peer to participate. If saving a contact normally triggers messages, provide a safe test route that suppresses delivery. A public request to “try our form” is too vague when the button can affect somebody outside the test.

Write down what the saved record should contain. In this example, the organization needs to be the contact's current company, which may differ from an older organization in an autofill profile. That difference gives the tester a reason to inspect and correct the suggestion rather than accept it automatically.

Use synthetic data and describe the browser conditions

Give the peer invented details that cannot be confused with a real customer. Use an address reserved for documentation where an email field is required, and keep outbound delivery disabled. Do not ask them to display their personal suggestion menu in a public recording.

Chrome's Autofill panel documentation describes inspecting address-field mappings and using provided test address data. That panel covers address information; it is not a complete test of every password manager, browser or input method.

Record the browser version, operating system and whether a browser feature or an extension supplied the values. Note whether the profile began with stored test data or used an offered test address. These conditions help another developer reproduce the observation without needing the original person's private setup.

A clean profile is useful for a repeatable case, but it is only one case. A returning user's older saved details may create different suggestions. Keep that as a separate follow-up with synthetic data, rather than quietly changing the conditions halfway through the first test.

Inspect the filled fields before touching them

Open the blank form and choose one available test suggestion. Observe which fields change. Read the displayed values, the required-field messages and the submit button's state. Avoid clicking through every field immediately, because that may trigger behavior that did not occur when autofill populated it.

The HTML autocomplete attribute gives browsers guidance about expected field values. MDN distinguishes values such as name, organization and email. Appropriate hints are a useful implementation check, but their presence does not prove that the whole product workflow works.

In the fictional case, suppose the name and email appear, while the form still says an email is required. Capture the visible contradiction. Then check whether focusing and leaving the email field changes the message. That sequence distinguishes the initial autofill result from a later interaction that may have caused the product to notice it.

Do not turn the workaround into the expected behavior. Requiring a person to touch an already filled field is a finding to investigate, even if it lets the test continue.

Correct one suggestion and follow the correction

Change the fictional organization's old name to the intended current name. Leave the other fields alone. Check whether the form recognizes the correction, whether any dependent summary updates, and whether a later browser suggestion unexpectedly replaces the edited value.

Next, submit once. Read the confirmation and reopen the contact through the normal product interface. Compare the displayed name, organization, email and address with the values reviewed just before submission. The result you need is the product's saved record, not the browser's memory of what it filled.

If the correction is missing, record exactly where the value changed. Was the old organization still visible before submission? Did the confirmation display the new one while the reopened record showed the old one? Different sequences point to different places for investigation.

This is where a developer's diagnostic work begins. The peer's report should preserve the observed sequence without guessing which event handler or state library caused it. A specific reproduction is more useful than a confident implementation theory attached to an incomplete screenshot.

Add a typed comparison and a recovery case

Reset the workspace, then create another synthetic contact by typing the same kind of values. Compare the field messages, button state and reopened record. Keep the input method as the main difference so the contrast remains interpretable.

If typing works and autofill does not, you have a narrower reproduction. You have not proved that all browser filling is broken. If both fail, the defect may belong to the broader form or save flow. Describe that result without forcing it into the original hypothesis.

Then test one relevant recovery. For example, leave a required field missing, submit, and use autofill or a manual correction to supply it. Check that the earlier error clears when the form accepts the value and that the final saved record is correct.

Avoid expanding the session into every possible form test. Keyboard order, duplicate submissions and network failure deserve their own checks. You can list those as untested boundaries while keeping this request focused on automatic filling, correction and persistence.

Give a peer a small test brief they can finish

A practical invitation names the test URL, disposable account, synthetic data, environment to record and expected saved result. State that no real customer information is needed. Explain where to report a mismatch and when to stop if the workflow leaves the safe test environment.

On Buildside, the founder community I founded, a public progress update can explain why you are checking this path and invite relevant developer feedback. Do not assume a general founder audience uses the browser combination you need. Ask for that condition explicitly, while making clear that participation is optional.

Keep private access details out of the public update. You can describe the task publicly and arrange approved test access separately. A usable invitation should let someone judge whether they can help without asking them to reveal their own stored information.

Thank the peer with a concrete resolution when the finding is addressed. Give them the revised test conditions and ask whether they want to recheck. A fresh test is more informative than assuming a code change removed the observed problem.

Publish the result at the level you actually checked

An honest update might say that an autofilled test email remained flagged as missing in one browser, and the revised form now saves the reviewed contact in that same reproduced case. Include the tested version and the remaining browser combinations you have not checked.

Show synthetic before-and-after values if they help explain the correction. Keep the browser suggestion menu out of the public image unless every visible detail is safe. Preserve meaningful field labels so another developer can understand what changed.

Autofill success is a sequence: a suggestion reaches the right fields, the user can inspect and correct it, validation reflects the current values, and the saved record contains the reviewed details. Building in public makes that sequence available for useful peer review. A full-looking form is only the beginning of the evidence.

Hey I'm Uriel Bitton. I write about building in public strategies and growing startups.

Subscribe for more stories on growing your audience by building in public.

Join us on Buildside: the social network for founders building in public.

articles.title: I built a background remover that runs 100% in the browser. Here's how I made it 7x faster
articles.description: Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you...
articles.body_html:
Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you to pay for the full-resolution download. I wanted the opposite: the photo never leaves your device, the download is full resolution, and there is no account.

So I built Remove de Fundo, a background remover where the AI model runs entirely in the browser. The first version worked, but on real phones it was slow enough that people left before seeing a result. This post is about what made it slow and what fixed it.

End result on the same laptop and the same photo: 43.8 s → 6.4 s from click to cutout.

The stack

  • Astro for the site (static pages, deployed to Cloudflare Workers)
  • @imgly/background-removal with the IS-Net fp16 model (~88 MB)
  • ONNX Runtime Web, which runs the model with WebGPU on desktop and WebAssembly (CPU) on phones
  • A small post-processing step in canvas to clean up semi-transparent "haze" in the mask

Everything happens client-side. The server only serves static files.

Problem 1: the model came from a CDN that didn't cache

The first visit downloads ~100 MB (model + ONNX runtime). That is unavoidable for an in-browser model, but I noticed something worse: the CDN serving the model sent no Cache-Control header, and the edge marked it cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC. So returning visitors were often downloading the model again, and nothing was cached near the user.

Fix: self-host the model files. A build script downloads the model chunks once and puts them in public/ai/<version>/, and the library is pointed there with publicPath. Since the chunk file names are content hashes, they can be cached forever:

/ai/*
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

Now a returning visitor loads the model from disk cache: zero network.

One gotcha: the chunk files have no extension, and both the dev server and the host treated extensionless paths as pages (404). Saving them as <hash>.bin and rewriting the names in resources.json fixed it.

Problem 2: the CPU path used one core out of eight

Phones always use the WebAssembly path, so CPU speed matters most. ONNX Runtime Web can use multiple threads, but only if the page is cross-origin isolated, because threads need SharedArrayBuffer.

My page wasn't isolated:

crossOriginIsolated // false

Fix: two headers.

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless

I used credentialless instead of require-corp so Google Fonts and analytics keep working without CORP headers. Browsers that don't support it simply ignore it, so nothing breaks there.

Result (CPU, model already loaded): 22.7 s → 7.9 s per photo. Almost 3x, from two lines of config.

Problem 3: the bug that made PNG encoding 13x slower

After enabling isolation, inference got much faster but the total barely improved. I logged a timestamp for each stage and found this:

Stage Time
Inference 1.5 s
PNG encode 5.5 s
Edge refinement 4.4 s

Encoding a 1200 × 800 PNG should take a fraction of a second. I measured canvas.convertToBlob() on an idle page:

Page PNG encode
Not isolated 208 ms
Isolated, before loading ONNX 217 ms
Isolated, after running ONNX 2,648 ms

So isolation itself was fine. The problem: the library sets the WASM thread count to navigator.hardwareConcurrency (all cores), and ONNX's worker threads keep spin-waiting after inference. They occupy every core, and the browser's own image-encoding threads starve.

Fix: cap the thread count before the library loads. I used ONNX Runtime's own default (half the cores, at most 4) on CPU, and 1 thread on the GPU path, where the GPU does the work:

function limitOnnxThreads(device: 'gpu' | 'cpu') {
  const cores = navigator.hardwareConcurrency || 4;
  const threads = device === 'gpu' ? 1 : Math.max(1, Math.min(4, Math.ceil(cores / 2)));
  Object.defineProperty(navigator, 'hardwareConcurrency', {
    configurable: true,
    get: () => threads,
  });
}

Post-processing went from ~10 s back to 0.2 s.

Problem 4: the first photo on WebGPU paid for shader compilation

On the WebGPU path, the second photo took 2 s but the first took ~17 s on every page load. The session creation and, mostly, the first inference compile the GPU shaders.

Fix: warm up on intent. When the user hovers the upload area (desktop) or taps it (mobile), I:

  1. Prefetch the model files into the HTTP cache (low priority).
  2. Call the library's preload() with exactly the same config as the real run (the library memoizes the session by JSON.stringify(config)).
  3. On GPU only, run one throwaway inference on a tiny 32×32 image. The model input has a fixed size, so this compiles everything the real photo needs.

While the person is still picking a photo from their gallery, all of that is already happening. I skip the warm inference on CPU: on a phone it would take as long as a real cutout and the user's photo would wait behind it. I also skip prefetching on saveData or 2G connections, and on mobile only a tap on the upload box triggers it, so scrolling past doesn't burn 100 MB of someone's data.

Things I tried that didn't work

  • The smaller quantized model (isnet_quint8, 44 MB). Half the download, but it left patches of background all over a portrait. Not worth it.
  • Relying on HTTP heuristic caching for a third-party CDN. In practice, returning visitors still re-downloaded.

UX fixes that mattered as much as speed

  • The upload box was below the fold on a 730 px laptop screen. People saw a headline and left. Tightening the hero put the button in the first screen on laptops and phones.
  • Show the user's own photo with a scanning line while processing, instead of a generic spinner. It makes the wait feel much shorter.
  • On mobile, the label "Drag your photo here" makes no sense. It now says "Choose a photo".

Results

Before After
Click → result (laptop, first run) 43.8 s 6.4 s
CPU inference per photo 22.7 s 7.9 s
PNG encode + edge cleanup ~10 s (isolated, before fix) 0.2 s
Returning visitor model download often ~100 MB 0 (disk cache)

Since adding analytics, about 98% of removals succeed and more than half of the people who upload a photo download the result.

Credits

The heavy lifting is done by IMG.LY's background-removal-js (AGPL-3.0) and ONNX Runtime Web. If you build something similar, check their licenses.

You can try it here: removedefundo.com/en. It's free, with no sign-up, and works in English, Spanish and Portuguese. I'd love feedback, especially from people on older phones.

This post was written with AI assistance. The numbers come from real measurements on the live site.

articles.title: My bot detector blocked 1 in 5 real humans. My tests said 1.4%.
articles.description: What I learned measuring a CAPTCHA-free bot detector against 120 real people instead of my own synthetic data, and the 7 fixes that went into Synapse Shield v0.11.0.
articles.body_html:
My open-source bot detector had a test suite with 950+ passing tests, a 1D-CNN, a Rust core with SIMD, and a README full of green checkmarks.

It was also blocking about 19% of real humans.

Not bots. People. Moving a mouse normally.

This post covers how I found that out, why my tests couldn't see it, and what changed in Synapse Shield v0.11.0. Every number below was measured before and after the change, on the same seeds.

🤔 What is Synapse Shield?

It's a self-hosted alternative to CAPTCHAs and Cloudflare Turnstile. It doesn't show puzzles. It looks at how a visitor moves, clicks and types, never what they type, and scores the session on your own server.

Setup is one line of middleware plus a small browser SDK:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from synapse_shield import SynapseShieldMiddleware

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(SynapseShieldMiddleware, protected_paths=["/api/login"])

<script src="/static/synapse-sdk.js"></script>
<script>
  SynapseShield.init();
  SynapseShield.protectFetch("/api/login");
</script>

That's the pitch. Now the uncomfortable part.

💥 The bug that hid behind a green test suite

The engine has five layers. One of them is a small 1D-CNN that looks at 60-step movement sequences.

On my machine its false-positive rate was 1.4%. That looked fine.

Then I replayed the public SapiMouse dataset (120 real people, real mouse recordings) through the exact weights that ship inside the package. Those are the weights a Docker deployment actually loads.

Real-human windows blocked What I thought What production did
6-second windows 1.4% 19.0%
20-second windows ~0.5% 19.2%

The cause took a while to see:

  1. The bundled weights had been trained only on synthetic Gaussian noise.
  2. My local runs loaded a different weights file from the working directory.
  3. A unit test (test_train.py) kept overwriting that local file with a model so saturated it was effectively switched off.

So the "1.4%" number came from a model that did nothing. The model my users would get was blocking one person in five.

The fix:

  • Weights now load in a fixed, explicit order: argument, then env var, then bundled file. A stray file in the working directory is ignored, with a warning.
  • Retraining refuses to write a saturated model.
  • The CNN now runs in shadow mode by default. It still scores every request and reports its raw score, but it can't block anyone until it earns that on real data.

Result: 19.0% → 1.4% (6 s) and 19.2% → 0.5% (20 s) on real people. Detection of the synthetic bots stayed at 100%.

💡 Lesson: a test suite proves your code does what you think. It doesn't prove what you think is true. Only real data does that.

🛠️ 6 more things real users taught me

Once I started measuring against real humans, the same pattern kept showing up. The rule looked reasonable, the synthetic tests passed, and it was still unfair to someone.

1. Touchscreen laptops were treated as liars

If the browser said "I support touch" but no touch events arrived, the session was marked as a spoofer.

A stricter penalty I tried would have blocked 100% of touch-laptop users and 71% of iPad-with-keyboard users. Those are normal devices.

Now such sessions are simply scored as desktop. I verified that the touch flag gives a bot no advantage: scores are identical with and without it.

2. Everyone behind one NAT was punished for one bot

Offices, universities and mobile carriers (CGNAT) put thousands of people behind one IP. One bot on that IP raised everyone's risk.

Now the short-term penalty is keyed to a hashed IP + User-Agent pair, and only hard violations count toward an IP ban. Under 60 requests per minute of mixed traffic, human loss went 2.47% → 0.08%. Scripted bots are still banned on their 4th request.

3. Short mouse movements looked "too perfect"

A single short flick of the mouse has very few points. Too few for curvature and frequency rules to mean anything.

50% of real single movements were blocked. Those rules now carry a capped weight on short traces, and borderline cases get a silent proof-of-work instead of a block. Result: 50.0% → 4.9%.

4. Pressing Enter looked like a bot click

When you press Enter on a form, Chrome fires a synthetic click at (0, 0). The engine saw a teleporting cursor.

Synthetic clicks within 50 ms of a key press are now ignored. In that scenario blocks went 100% → 5.4%.

5. Replaying a real human recording worked every time

This one's the attacker's side. If you record a real person's mouse trace and replay it from a fresh IP and User-Agent, it really does look human.

v0.11.0 adds two defences, neither of which stores raw traces:

  • a keyed 64-bit trajectory fingerprint, consumed only when a request is allowed;
  • a session shape hash (SimHash) that survives scaling, noise and time warping.

A recorded trace replayed with fresh IPs was allowed 100% → 10% of the time, and only on its first use. In-session repeats are caught from the 3rd request. Measured human false positives: 0.02%.

6. Some client signals could only help the attacker

A few browser-side hints lowered the risk score, for example a flag claiming "this is a common letter pair". Anything the client sends can be forged.

The rule now: client signals can only raise risk, never lower it. Real-typist false positives on the CMU keystroke dataset didn't change (0.034%).

❌ What I didn't ship (and why)

Some ideas looked good on paper and failed when measured:

  • Tremor detection via an FFT frequency band: it cost bot detection and didn't fix the people it was meant to help.
  • Extra keystroke rules: at most 8% more bots caught at a 0.5% real-human false-positive cost. Not worth it.
  • Fail-closed on a Redis outage: it sounds secure, but it turns a cache hiccup into a self-inflicted outage. Fail-open is now documented instead.

Deleting a feature you spent a day on is painful. Shipping one that blocks real people is worse.

🧾 Honest limits

I'd rather you hear these from me than find them in production:

  • All bot numbers are synthetic. Human false-positive numbers come from real public datasets, but I have no labelled real-bot traffic yet. Read "100% detection" as "catches these generators".
  • About 18% of very short (3–10 point) single movements are still blocked.
  • Sophisticated replay still works partly. An attacker who records many real sessions and replays each one once with small changes looks human to the behavioural layer. The system raises their cost; it isn't a wall. Keep rate limits and MFA.
  • The plain-JS protectFetch doesn't auto-solve proof-of-work challenges yet. The React and Vue SDKs do (submitProtected()).

🚀 Try it 

pip install "synapse-shield[server]"
synapse-shield run --port 8000

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 for the live dashboard, then run synapse-shield test in a second terminal to throw the built-in attack simulations at it.

Not ready to block anyone yet? Turn on shadow mode. It scores real traffic and reports what would have been blocked, per device cohort, without touching a single user.

👉 GitHub: 0xStoic-bit/Synapse_Shield (MIT, Python 3.10–3.14, prebuilt wheels for Linux, macOS and Windows)

💬 Over to you

I'm curious about two things:

  1. Have you ever shipped a security rule that turned out to punish real users? How did you find out?
  2. Does anyone have labelled real bot traffic (even a small sample) that could be used to test bot detection honestly? It's the biggest gap in this project.

If this saved you from one more "select all traffic lights" puzzle, a ⭐ on GitHub helps other developers find it.

articles.title: The Most Dangerous AI-Generated Test Is the One That Passes
articles.description: AI can generate a browser test in seconds.  You give it a URL and ask it to verify that the search...
articles.body_html:
AI can generate a browser test in seconds.

You give it a URL and ask it to verify that the search feature works. It opens the page, enters a search term, checks that some results appear, and produces a test.

You execute it. Green.

You run it ten more times. Still green.

Then a customer reports that the search results disappear when they press the browser's Back button.

Your automated test never caught it.

The problem wasn't that the AI generated invalid code. The code worked exactly as written.

The problem was that nobody questioned what the test was actually proving.

And I think this is one of the biggest risks with the current wave of AI-powered test automation.

A passing test doesn't necessarily mean a working feature

Let's take a typical e-commerce application.

The search page has a few common behaviors:

  • Results update after the user stops typing.
  • The search query is reflected in the URL.
  • Refreshing the page preserves the search.
  • Opening a product and pressing Back restores the previous results.
  • Slow API responses don't cause stale results to appear.

A human tester familiar with the application might consider all five behaviors important.

But ask an AI agent to "test the product search," and it might generate something like this:

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product search works', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  await page.getByPlaceholder('Search products')
    .fill('wireless');

  await expect(
    page.getByText('Wireless Headset')
  ).toBeVisible();
});

Is this a valid test?

Sure.

Does it prove that product search works?

Only in a very narrow sense.

It doesn't verify the URL, navigation history, request ordering, or what happens when the page is refreshed.

And because the test passes, the team might never notice those missing scenarios.

The missing assertions are more dangerous than flaky assertions

Flaky tests get attention because they interrupt CI pipelines.

Missing assertions are quieter.

They don't fail. They don't generate alerts. They don't slow down deployments.

They simply leave important behavior untested.

Consider a search field that uses debouncing.

If a user types "wireless headset," the application might wait 300 milliseconds after the last keystroke before sending the search request.

This reduces unnecessary API calls.

But now imagine two requests arrive out of order.

The user searches for "wireless," then quickly changes the term to "wireless headset."

The newer request completes first. The correct results appear.

A moment later, the older request completes and replaces them with results for "wireless."

The UI is now showing stale data.

A basic test might miss this entirely.

Similarly, the application might display the correct results but fail to synchronize the URL, making its search state impossible to preserve through navigation.

The guide Testing Debounced Search, URL Sync, and Back-Button State Without Flaky Assertions covers these kinds of scenarios and explains why outcome-based assertions are generally more reliable than hard-coded delays.

Here's a more useful browser test for an application where search state is stored in the URL:

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search survives navigation and refresh', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  const search = page.getByRole('searchbox', {
    name: /search/i
  });

  await search.fill('wireless');

  // Verify that search state reaches the URL.
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/products\?q=wireless$/);

  // Verify a meaningful search result.
  const product = page.getByRole('link', {
    name: 'Wireless Headset'
  });

  await expect(product).toBeVisible();

  // Navigate to the product and return.
  await product.click();
  await page.goBack();

  // The previous search should be restored.
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/products\?q=wireless$/);
  await expect(search).toHaveValue('wireless');
  await expect(product).toBeVisible();

  // Refresh should preserve the same state.
  await page.reload();

  await expect(search).toHaveValue('wireless');
  await expect(product).toBeVisible();
});

This example assumes the application provides these accessibility labels and URL conventions.

Notice what's missing from the test: waitForTimeout(300).

We're testing the behavior, not the implementation detail of how long the debounce timer takes.

That makes the test both more useful and less sensitive to timing differences.

It still doesn't cover out-of-order API responses. That deserves a separate test with controlled response ordering.

The point is that a good suite covers distinct risks, rather than generating multiple variations of the same happy path.

What if the UI is correct but the API contract has changed?

Here's another problem that AI-generated browser tests can miss.

Suppose the search API used to return:

{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "Wireless Headset",
  "price": 79.99
}

After a backend update, it starts returning:

{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "Wireless Headset",
  "price": "79.99"
}

The price field changed from a number to a string.

The browser might still render $79.99 correctly.

Your end-to-end test passes.

But another consumer of that API might fail because it expects a numeric value.

This is schema drift, and it's one reason browser tests shouldn't be your only line of defense.

A useful API testing strategy should verify response contracts, not just HTTP status codes.

It should also help teams reproduce failures using mocks or stubs, and preserve enough information to explain why a CI run failed.

There's a practical selection rubric in Schema Drift, Mock Support, and CI Failure Evidence: What to Look for in API Testing Tools.

You don't need to perform every assertion through a browser.

In fact, trying to force all testing into the end-to-end layer usually makes your suite slower and more expensive to maintain.

The browser should verify what the user experiences. API and contract tests should verify the assumptions that different services make about each other.

AI should generate drafts, not unquestionable truth

This brings us back to AI.

The promise is attractive: generate automated tests from natural-language instructions, reduce scripting work, and create broader coverage faster.

There's real value in that.

But the part that deserves more attention is what happens after the test is generated.

Can someone read the steps?

Can they modify an assertion?

Can they understand why the AI chose a particular action?

Can they reject a generated test before it becomes part of the release pipeline?

And if the AI modifies an existing test to accommodate a UI change, can someone review that modification?

Imagine an automated test failing because the Checkout button disappeared.

An AI self-healing mechanism might find another button and successfully click it.

That's useful if the button was simply renamed.

It's dangerous if the AI silently selected a different action.

A previously failing test can become green without the underlying problem being fixed.

The article Human Review Is the Feature: Choosing AI Testing Tools That Keep You in Control examines exactly these considerations, including editable steps, approval workflows, rollback capabilities, and the evidence available to reviewers.

For most teams, I think the sensible approach is straightforward.

Use AI to accelerate test creation and maintenance.

But keep the expected behavior, critical assertions, and acceptance criteria under human control.

The goal should be to reduce repetitive work, not remove accountability.

More tests also means more test management

There's a less exciting consequence of AI-generated automation.

Once generating tests becomes cheap, teams can end up with thousands of them.

Some are duplicates.

Some validate trivial behavior.

Some are based on outdated requirements.

Others were generated for features that no longer exist.

And someone eventually has to figure out which tests matter.

This is where test management becomes important.

Not because every automated test needs a lengthy approval process, but because a team needs some way to connect test cases with requirements, ownership, execution results, and releases.

Tools such as Qase and TestRail approach that problem differently.

The comparison Qase vs TestRail: Less Process Overhead Without Losing Test Visibility examines the tradeoff between a lighter workflow and more structured test management.

That distinction becomes increasingly relevant when AI generates tests faster than people can review them.

A small team might need a lightweight system that makes it easy to organize cases and eliminate duplication.

A larger organization might need stricter controls around ownership, revisions, and release reporting.

Either way, generating additional tests isn't automatically equivalent to improving coverage.

A suite with 500 carefully maintained tests can be more valuable than a suite with 5,000 tests nobody fully understands.

In regulated environments, green isn't enough

The stakes change when automated tests are used in healthcare, financial services, insurance, or other regulated environments.

Imagine an AI agent modifies a test covering a payment approval workflow.

The updated test passes.

Six months later, an auditor asks:

Who modified the test?

Why was it changed?

Who approved the modification?

Which version executed before the release?

What evidence was preserved?

A screenshot showing a green checkmark won't answer those questions.

Organizations with formal audit requirements need traceability across test creation, modification, approval, execution, and evidence retention.

That's why choosing an AI testing platform for a regulated environment involves more than comparing how effectively the tools generate tests.

The guide Regulated Teams Need Different AI Testing Platforms looks at audit logs, approval workflows, role-based permissions, evidence export, and retention policies.

Not every product needs those controls.

A small SaaS startup can usually operate with much less ceremony.

But for regulated teams, the ability to reconstruct what happened during a release may be just as important as the test result itself.

And introducing AI into the workflow doesn't eliminate those requirements.

It makes clearly defined responsibilities even more important.

A simple rule for reviewing AI-generated tests

Before accepting an AI-generated test into a production test suite, I'd ask the reviewer to answer four questions.

1. What user behavior does this test actually prove?

Not what the test is called. Not what the prompt asked the AI to generate. What does the execution really verify?

2. Could the feature be broken while this test still passes?

Think about stale data, missing persistence, wrong API responses, navigation behavior, and alternative paths.

This question alone often reveals missing assertions.

3. If the test fails, will someone understand why?

A useful test should produce enough context to investigate the problem without spending an hour reproducing it manually.

4. Can we safely review and reverse changes to the test?

This matters especially when AI tools can modify existing tests or update locators automatically.

If the generated test cannot pass these four questions, it probably isn't ready to become part of your regression suite.

The real opportunity with AI in testing

I don't think AI-generated test automation is a bad idea.

Quite the opposite.

Creating automated tests has traditionally required too much repetitive work, especially when translating human-readable test cases into scripts.

AI can help reduce that effort substantially.

But I wouldn't measure success by the number of tests an AI agent generates.

I'd look at how many meaningful failures those tests catch, how much time they save during maintenance, and how quickly engineers can investigate failures.

Most importantly, I'd look at whether the team understands what its tests are actually validating.

Because there's a big difference between automating a browser interaction and proving that a feature works.

AI is making the first one much easier.

The second one still requires engineering judgment.

And that's probably a good thing.

articles.title: The Week My App Almost Ran Out of Database
articles.description: Hey dev.to — Lepp again. Entry two in building Neuro-Kindred (a free, calm social app for...
articles.body_html:
Hey dev.to — Lepp again. Entry two in building Neuro-Kindred (a free, calm social app for neurodivergent adults, 18+) in the open. Last time: pebbles instead of likes. This time: a mystery, three wrong suspects, and the week I nearly lost the whole app to a free-tier limit.

The setup

Neuro-Kindred runs on a $3/month server and a free Postgres database (Neon, 100 free compute-hours a month). On Nov 15 I got the email nobody wants: 80 of the 100 hours already used, halfway through the month. At 100, the database sleeps until December 1st — app down, no charge, data safe, but down.

Something was waking the database constantly. It wasn't my members: in the worst 48-hour stretch, 38 members sent 63 messages total. So I went hunting.

Suspect #1: the scanners

The server logs showed a burst of 188 requests in one minute from a cloud IP, probing for .env files and admin paths. All 404s, nothing exposed — but bots were my first theory. Verdict: real, but too small. The burn continued on quiet nights with no scanner traffic at all.

Suspect #2: the old deployment

The app used to live on an app-builder platform before I moved it to my own server. Maybe the old copy was still running somewhere, pinging away? I unpublished it (Nov 17) and measured for 24 hours. The burn barely moved. Not the culprit — and now I couldn't easily un-unpublish my main suspect.

Suspect #3: my own forgotten robots

This one stung. Back in September, the builder era set up two keep-alive jobs (duplicates, of course) pinging the app's health endpoint every 5 minutes — and every ping runs database queries, and every query resets the database's 5-minute idle timer. The database was being politely woken up 24/7 by robots I owned. I disabled both (Nov 15) and the sleep test passed... but the daily burn only dropped a little. A contributor. Not the culprit.

The actual culprit: the app itself

The final measurement read the request logs by endpoint. In 48 hours: the calls screen had been checked 3,497 times — about once every 3 seconds — from one or two phones with the page left open. Message threads every 4–5 seconds. Game rooms every 2 seconds. My own app's screens were the waker. One member leaving the app open on their phone was costing more database than every real conversation combined.

The fix shipped Nov 20: the calls overview now checks every 20 seconds, message threads every 10 (pausing entirely when the tab is hidden was already in there — the problem was never hidden tabs, it was visible ones being impatient). Full test suite green (552 tests), and I'm re-measuring for 24 hours before I claim it worked. If the number doesn't drop, I'll say so in entry three.

The honest numbers

  • Database: 86.3 of 100 free hours used (Nov 18 reading)
  • Members: 38 · Revenue: $0 · Server: $3/month
  • Cost of the investigation: a few evenings and one unpublished old site

Lesson: on a free tier, your own polling is your biggest user. Measure by endpoint before you blame the internet.

One question before you go

Neuro-Kindred runs a community night every Friday, 7pm CT (trivia, a game, then a watch-together on Discord) — it's the hour the app feels most like itself. Comment with the interest you could talk about for a full hour, and I'll send you an invite to this Friday's. That's the whole exchange — your weird topic for a seat at the table. It's also literally what the app is for.

— Lepp

Next entry: "Pebbles grow old now" — why an unanswered pebble sitting in limbo forever is unkind, and the 30-day close we just shipped.

articles.title: Your Sticky Header Is Hiding Anchor Links. `scroll-margin-top` Fixes It.
articles.description: Clicking a table-of-contents link lands the heading right behind your sticky nav, half-hidden. The fix isn't a JavaScript scroll offset — it's one CSS property the browser already checks before it scrolls.
articles.body_html:
You redesign a docs page. Sticky header, clean table of contents down the side, the kind of polish that makes a demo look finished. Then someone clicks "Installation" in the TOC, and the page jumps — except the "Installation" heading is now sitting behind the header, top third clipped off, like the scroll stopped one beat too early.

It's not a bug in your heading. It's not a bug in the TOC link. The browser scrolled exactly where you told it to. You just never told it about the header.

The obvious fix that didn't quite work

The TOC links are plain anchors: <a href="#installation">. The browser handles the jump on its own — no JavaScript required, which is exactly why it feels like it shouldn't need any. So the first fix is the one that feels native to the problem: intercept the click, do the math yourself.

document.querySelectorAll('a[href^="#"]').forEach((link) => {
  link.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const id = link.getAttribute("href").slice(1);
    const target = document.getElementById(id);
    const headerHeight = document.querySelector("header").offsetHeight;
    window.scrollTo({
      top: target.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY - headerHeight - 16,
      behavior: "smooth",
    });
  });
});

It works. Click a TOC link, the heading lands below the header, clean. Ship it, close the ticket.

Then QA files three more:

  • Deep-linking straight to yoursite.com/docs#installation — no click ever fired — still lands the heading behind the header, because the hack only runs on click.
  • The browser's native back/forward button restores the old scroll position, not yours — hitting Back after a TOC click snaps right back behind the header.
  • Mobile ships a taller header. headerHeight was read once on load; resize the window and the offset is stale until a reload.

Each of those is a separate bug with a separate fix — handle DOMContentLoaded for the deep-link case, listen for popstate, re-read offsetHeight on resize. You're not patching one bug anymore. You're reimplementing the browser's own "scroll to this element" logic, one missed case at a time, in a <script> tag.

The browser already asks "how much space do you need"

Fragment navigation, Element.scrollIntoView(), and the browser scrolling a focused element into view as you tab through the page all go through the same question: what counts as "this element is now in view"? Since 2021, every major browser has agreed on an answer CSS checks before any of them run — scroll-margin-top and its counterpart, scroll-padding-top.

Put it on the headings themselves:

h2,
h3 {
  scroll-margin-top: 4.5rem; /* roughly the header's height, plus breathing room */
}

That's it. No click handler, no preventDefault(), no recomputed pixel offset. Click a TOC link, hit the browser's native back button, paste a #installation link straight into the address bar — every path the browser uses to bring that heading into view now stops 4.5rem early, because the browser itself is doing the arithmetic, the same way it always has.

Per-heading vs. whole-page: pick the one that matches the bug

scroll-margin-top goes on the target — the thing being scrolled to. scroll-padding-top goes on the scroll container — usually html, or whatever element actually scrolls — and applies the same offset to every target inside it, without touching each heading individually:

html {
  scroll-padding-top: 4.5rem; /* one declaration, covers every #anchor on the site */
}

If every page on the site sits under the same sticky header, scroll-padding-top on html is the one-line, whole-site fix — set it once, forget it. Reach for scroll-margin-top on specific elements instead when different targets need different offsets: a shorter mobile header, a taller "in-page alert" banner above certain sections, or a card in a horizontally-scrolling carousel that needs its own left-edge margin rather than a top one.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Stop hardcoding the header's height as a magic number

4.5rem is a guess that goes stale the day someone adds a banner to the header. Read the header's real height instead, and feed it in as a custom property:

:root {
  --header-h: 64px; /* kept in sync with the header's actual rendered height */
}

h2,
h3 {
  scroll-margin-top: calc(var(--header-h) + 16px);
}

const header = document.querySelector("header");
const setHeaderHeight = () =>
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--header-h", `${header.offsetHeight}px`);

setHeaderHeight();
new ResizeObserver(setHeaderHeight).observe(header);

Now the only JavaScript left is measuring the header — not re-deriving the browser's entire scroll-to-element behavior. If the header grows a second row on mobile, ResizeObserver catches it and the custom property updates; scroll-margin-top reads the new value on the next scroll. The division of labor is the point: JavaScript's job shrinks to "report one number," and CSS's job — "stop scrolling here" — stays where the browser already does it for free.

Where this still needs a human

scroll-margin-top fixes where the page lands. It doesn't fix a heading that's visually ambiguous about whether it's "the current section" once it's sitting right under the header edge — that's a design question about header contrast and spacing, not a CSS-property question. And if your TOC also needs to highlight the active section as the reader scrolls, that's a separate job (usually IntersectionObserver), not something scroll-margin-top does for you. It solves exactly one problem — stopping short of the header — and it's worth not asking it to solve the other two.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The bug report wasn't "the table of contents is broken." It was "the browser doesn't know about your header" — and it turns out the browser was willing to be told, in CSS, for free, since before most of us noticed. Got a scroll offset hack sitting in a click handler somewhere? Go check what it's actually compensating for — there's a decent chance one property replaces it.

articles.title: `npm ci` Doesn't Fix the .npmrc Override. It Just Hides It Better.
articles.description: Ana cloned the repo on a Friday afternoon, the way everyone on her team does it now. Clean folder,...
articles.body_html:
Ana cloned the repo on a Friday afternoon, the way everyone on her team does it now. Clean folder, fresh clone, one command she trusts more than the old one, because the team switched to it months ago for exactly this reason: no surprises. The output said one line, added 1 package, and she moved on. Monday morning she found a file in the package folder that should not have been there, stamped Friday afternoon, written by a hook she believed she had switched off years ago in her own config file. Nothing had warned her. Nothing had even whispered. The install had done exactly what it was told to do by a file she had never opened, and the one line of output had hidden all of it.

That is the part people keep getting wrong about npm ci. It feels safer than npm install. It wipes the folder, it reads the lockfile, it refuses to improvise. All of that is true, and none of it touches the question that actually bit Ana. The question is not whether the install is clean. The question is whose word it takes when two config files disagree, and whether you would ever find out.

maxbuildsdev asked me that in the comments on my last piece: does the layering hold the same way under npm ci, with a lockfile in play, and does the foreground flag show a hook running instead of swallowing it? Same trap, same two config files, same tiny test package with one install hook that leaves a marker file behind. Fourteen installs, two runs per shape, and I wrote down what actually happened.

1. The lockfile changes nothing about who wins

This was the question, and the answer is blunt: the repo still wins. Plain npm ci inside the repo ran the hook both times, markers stamped 00:09:25 and 00:09:35 UTC. Plain npm ci in the clean folder, the same package with no repo file of its own, ran it neither time. The CLI flag kept it off both times in the repo. Twelve installs in the main matrix, two repeats per shape, and not one repeat disagreed with its twin.

I had half expected the lockfile to matter. It is the whole point of ci, after all: the install is supposed to follow the lockfile and nothing else. But the lockfile only pins which packages and versions get installed. It says nothing about whether their install hooks are allowed to run. That decision still comes from the config layers, and the layers still stack the same way they did under plain npm install: the file sitting in the repo beats the file sitting in your home folder, every time, without a word about it. If you switched to ci because you thought the lockfile closed this hole, you switched to a stricter installer for a problem it was never built to solve.

2. Silence is not proof, and ci is quieter than most

Here is the part that should bother you more than the override itself. In both repo installs, the hook ran and the output said nothing at all. One line: added 1 package. No hook name, no hook output, no hint that anything besides the install had happened. The only proof was the marker file sitting in the package folder afterwards, which nobody looks for on a normal Friday.

That is the same silence plain npm install gave me in November, and it lands harder under ci for a simple reason: ci is the command people reach for when they want certainty. The whole pitch is that nothing unexpected happens. So when the output comes back clean, people read it as confirmation that nothing unexpected happened. It is not confirmation. It is just a quiet log. A hook can run, write files, print nothing, and leave you with an output line that reads like a clean bill of health. If your evidence that hooks are off is "the install looked fine," you have no evidence.

3. The foreground flag is a witness, not a guard

This is the one piece of good news, and it comes with a catch worth naming plainly. Run the same install with the foreground flag and the hook stops being invisible. Both repo runs printed the hook out in the open:

> hook-test-pkg@1.0.0 preinstall
> node -e "require('fs').writeFileSync('HOOK-RAN.txt', ...); console.log('HOOK-RAN-MARKER preinstall executed')"

HOOK-RAN-MARKER preinstall executed

There it is, the hook's own printed line, in the output where you can actually see it. After two rounds of installs where the hook ran in total silence, watching it finally announce itself felt like the tool apologising. But a witness is all it is. The flag never stopped a hook. In the clean folder, where my user setting already blocks hooks, the flag changed nothing, both times. And with both flags together in the repo, the hook stayed off both times: the ignore flag still beats the foreground flag. So the foreground flag answers one question, did a hook run and what did it say, and no other. If you add it hoping it will protect you, you have bought a window, not a lock, and a window helps only if someone is looking through it at the exact moment the install runs.

4. The check lies unless it stands next to the install

cryptostrapon added the edge that makes the other three problems actually dangerous, and it is the one I keep thinking about. The check I have been recommending, npm config list inside the repo, tells the truth. Run it from the folder above the repo and it tells you something else entirely: my user value, true, with no project section at all, no mention that a repo file even exists. Same machine, seconds apart, two opposite answers, and both are correct about the folder they were asked in.

Then I split the check and the install apart on purpose, the way a build job does when the check lives in one step and the install in a later one. Check at the root said true, safe. The later install in the repo ran the hook anyway, marker stamped 00:11:13 UTC. And the mirror image: check inside the repo said false, hook will run, and the later install in the clean folder ran nothing at all.

That is how this trap actually gets built in real teams. Nobody skips the check. They run it in the wrong folder, or in an earlier step with its own working directory, read the green answer, and walk into an install that answers to a different file. The fix is not a better check. It is a check that refuses to live anywhere except right next to the install: same folder, same step, immediately before npm ci. Anything further away is a reading about a different place.

So here is where I land. npm ci does not fix the override. It just hides it better, behind a lockfile and a one-line summary that both feel like safety and neither is. The repo file still wins, the hook still runs in silence, and the only flag that shows it is a witness that cannot stop it. The CLI flag still wins when you type it, and the check still tells the truth when it stands in the right folder at the right moment.

What do you run before you install a repo you did not write? The check in the repo folder, the CLI flag every time, or do you trust the lockfile and the one-line output like Ana did on that Friday? Tell me what your setup actually does, not what it is supposed to do. I want to know which of these four problems has bitten you, and whether the bite came from the override, the silence, or a check that was read in the wrong folder.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.description: Hoi hoi! 😸  Happy Friday! Let's learn a tiny bit of Rust! 😸🍻  No complicated architecture. No giant...
articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi! 😸

Happy Friday! Let's learn a tiny bit of Rust! 😸🍻

No complicated architecture. No giant diagrams. Just a cat, a crab, and a little bit of ownership.

Grab a beer! 🍺

🐈 Ownership::This Is My Cat!

Rust has three simple ownership rules:

  • Every value has an owner.
  • There can only be one owner at a time.
  • When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.

Let's adopt a cat!

let a = String::from("cat");
let b = a;

println!("{b}");

📦 Move::Wait... Where's My Cat?!

What happens if we try to use a again?

println!("{a}"); // ❌ Compile error!

WHAT?! WHERE IS MY CAT?! 🙀

Ownership moved from a to b.

Sorry, a. That's not your cat anymore. 😿

Rust remembers. Rust never forgets. 🦀

Small note: This behavior applies to non-Copy types like String. Simple types such as i32 implement Copy, so let b = a; copies the value and a can still be used. 😸

🤝 Borrowing::Can I Pet Your Cat?

What if we just want to borrow a value without taking ownership?

We can use a reference (&).

let a = String::from("cat");
let b = &a;

println!("{b}");
println!("{a}");

WOW! Both work! 😸

a still owns the value. b is just borrowing it.

You can pet my cat, but you can't take it home. 😼

✏️ MutableBorrowing::The Cats Are Multiplying!

A shared reference (&) doesn't let us modify the borrowed String.

But a mutable reference (&mut) does!

let mut a = String::from("cat");

let b = &mut a;
b.push_str(" and another cat");

println!("{a}");

Output 👇

cat and another cat

Oh no.

The cats are multiplying. 🐈🐈

🦀 BorrowChecker::One Human at a Time!

Multiple humans can pet the same cat.

let cat = String::from("cat");

let a = &cat;
let b = &cat;

println!("{a} {b}"); // ✅

Everyone is happy. The cat gets extra attention. 😸

But what if two humans try to brush the same cat at once?

let mut cat = String::from("cat");

let a = &mut cat;
let b = &mut cat; // ❌ Compile error!

a.push_str(" is fluffy");
b.push_str(" is SUPER fluffy");

Rust::ABSOLUTELY NOT. 🦀💢

So here's the rule:

  • & — Many humans can borrow the cat for reading.
  • &mut — Only one human can borrow the cat for modification, with no other active borrows.

Want to brush the cat? Wait until everyone else is done borrowing it!

The crab is just trying to keep our cats safe. 🐈💚

🍪 Summary::One Little Byte at a Time

  • Ownership -> This is my cat.
  • Move -> It's your cat now.
  • & -> You can pet my cat.
  • &mut -> You can brush my cat, but one human at a time.
  • BorrowChecker -> The angry crab protecting our cats. 🦀

That's it for today's Cozy Bytes!

Rust looks scary sometimes, but we don't have to learn everything at once.

One little byte at a time. 😸💚

Happy Friday! 🍻

articles.title: I Haven't Written a Line of Code in Months. And I Don't Know How to Feel About It.
articles.description: Introduction   It's been a while since I wrote something here. It feels like it was a...
articles.body_html:
Introduction

It's been a while since I wrote something here. It feels like it was a lifetime ago. Our world, and especially our programming world, moves so fast that I can't recognize the way it was 6 years ago, 2 years ago, or even at the beginning of this year. So, I wanted to write down some thoughts and see where they take me.

Dealing with changes

In our line of work, we're used to changes right? New languages, new technologies, new frameworks... we've always had new things to look forward to, or being scared of, learn, hate... But this AI stuff... Damn, it's not just something new, it's the first time I've actually felt threatened, in danger, overwhelmed.

It's a very strange feeling because I have the feeling like we are at the edge of a new world, full of possibilities, adventures, discoveries. Things that we thought would take us weeks, months, or years to do or solve become doable so much faster. In the field of science, we see cool stuff happening. And even if I don't understand anything about it, it looks cool to discover new proofs and solutions, even if it's AI assisted. But...

What about me?

I'm a good developer ok? I'm not a rockstar, but I've some strenghts. I've always enjoyed learning new stuff about design patterns, how to write good code. Less than a year ago, I was still learning new things, trying to write more elegant code. I was happy when I found a beautiful solution to a problem.

Around March this year, our team decided it was time to equip everyone with Claude. I don't think I've written a line of code since then. How insane is that? Most of my time was spent in writing code, and now, it has completely disappeared from my tasks. So now, I'm mostly managing agents and doing all the conception and planning. That's where my "expertise" comes in. Because this stuff writes much better code than me anyway.

I feel... dizzy.

What about my (our) future?

The one thing that is scary is not knowing to me. I don't know what our jobs will look like next year, in 2 years, in 10 years. Will we still have a job? How will it look? I'm not much into the doom prediction like "Developers will be gone in 6 months". But something is gonna change drastically right? What about the juniors, the people entering the job market today?

It's not all bad of course. It's not. It's the uncertainty that's difficult for me.

I'm building a very cool project with a few colleagues and AI allowed us to move a lot faster than we would have on our own. That's really exciting. Being able to deliver features a lot faster to users is always a nice feeling. That's one of the main reasons I started doing this anyway, help people.

Loss of craftsmanship

When I wrote the code, with my slow hands, I felt like a craftsman. I was building something. The code was mine. Now, it's not. It's industrialized. A machine makes it. Like countless other craftsmen in the history of our species, what I used to do with my hands in hours or days is done by a machine in minutes.

It's a strange feeling. Of course, I try to comfort myself. I still need to pilot this thing. It doesn't have my humanity, it doesn't know my users like I know them. I have better business knowledge than this machine. And in the end, it's always me that makes the final decision. For how long? And how much value does it have?

This is also why I write this. Because I can still sit in front of my computer and pour out the words. My words. From my brain and my heart. It feels good to create something all by yourself. And I still have the hope that whatever the future holds for us, we will build cool stuff to help people. I hope that the AI era that we're entering will be a net positive for humanity.

Conclusion

That's it, that was my little rant. I'll keep building things that I believe will help people to better their lives and jobs. We will see, together, where this new world takes us.

Have fun <3
