Introduction

In this article, I'll expose an issue we had in one of my freelance missions, what we learned from it and how it started our journey towards building our own system.

Disclaimer: I am one of the co-founders of Notifizz, a unified notification platform that leverages AI to give marketing teams autonomy in handling their notifications.

The problem

Our architecture was composed of several microservices. One of them was handling the notifications: receiving requests and calling whatever third party service was responsible for sending a message.

Marketing teams designed notifications to achieve certain goals: alerting a customer of a new invoice, reminding him of an important task, informing about a new functionality... Each notification exists , or should exist, to achieve a business goal.

Obviously, there is no guarantee that a notification will allow the company to achieve whatever goal they set right away. You track an objective related to a notification, and you see if users do the action you intended them to do from that notification.

What if it doesn't work? Or doesn't work well enough? Marketing might want to make a few changes. Adjust the wording. Perhaps send the notification at a different moment in the process. Or maybe send an email AND an in-app message...

And that's the first hurdle. For every change, marketing needs to either have a little bit of experience with certain tools (we used mailgun for example, which isn't the most straightforward piece of technology for non-devs) or send a ticket to the dev team to implement the changes. The marketing team is completely dependent on the dev team. It loses time and possibly keeps a suboptimal campaign live while the dev team finds the time to do the changes and push it to prod.

A solution?

So we thought (back in 2023), what if the marketing team had complete control over their campaigns? What if they were completely independent from the dev team? How would that look like?

You still need developers in the loop, obviously. But we thought that we could create everything we needed in our application beforehand (events, endpoints...) like building blocks, and let the marketing team construct their campaigns like this.

Our application would emit events. For instance, a new invoice is created -> event invoice.created, emitted from the microservice responsible for invoicing. That microservice would publish this event and its payload to a pub/sub topic.

So far, so good. But now you need an interface right? Because marketing wants to create a campaign to alert clients about the invoice. And the marketing team doesn't know anything about code, or what's an API or a microservice... And they need something flexible so that they add a new field if necessary, or update the wording...

So we thought about adding Make. Make lets you create scenarios and chain modules in a sequence. It takes an input (in our case, it would take our pub/sub' subscription) and you can chain different modules to manipulate data.

And because you can create custom modules in Make, we created modules that allowed us to call our API, so we could enrich the original event payload input with data from some of our other microservices. That way, we thought, even if marketing is missing a field, they will use one of our pre-designed modules and add it themselves, without the devs! Genius!

Right? Input's data -> call one or several modules to enrich -> call our notification microservice to send the notification.

Well, it was a disaster.

Why it didn't work

First, the payload you get from the event is a JSON, and it needs to be parsed for the Make scenario to know it and manipulate it. So right off the bat, you're adding a JSON concept into a process that's supposed to be developers free.

Second, if you call our API, you need to think about security. So you need to pass a token, or an api key or something from Make to make sure your data is not being called from anyone. Another concept that's not marketing friendly.

Third, you actually need a lot of JSON manipulating in that use case inside Make. Too much for a non technical person to use. The whole point was to make sure you didn't need to be a developer to use that process.

A "simple" scenario could look like this

Fourth, the variety of tools used complicated things. Because everything was spread out across different tools (templates were in Mailgun, the team used Intercom, Mailchimp, plus Make ...), it was impossible to teach the marketing team to be fully autonomous in the process. It would have been way too costly to train them on these tools to handle everything like we expected. It wasn't their job anyway.

Fifth, we also needed to handle different environments. Obviously, you don't send your notifications to production right off the bat. You need to test them locally, then test them in a deployed environment then finally you push it to production. In our case, we needed to have a different scenario for each environment (different pub/sub subscription/topic, different modules).

What we learned

Lack of control

No-code, at least in 2023 the way we used it became a growing problem saying: You need to adapt everything to us and our way of things, not the other way around. And it became clear that the level of complexity would be way too expensive to implement and maintain with the available tools in order to achieve the marketing autonomy goals we had.

The expertise needed

You can't remove developers entirely from that loop. At one point or another, you need a developer to implement some code (an endpoint to enrich, a new event, a new field in an existing event ...). So the problem became more of: how do we clearly separate dev tasks from marketing tasks so that each team does what it's good at, without making each other lose too much time?

To do that, we think, we need to have a centralized interface where everything was easier to follow and monitor. In one place, designing your email, in-app or intercom messages, track deliverability, events and their payloads and where in the development process is the campaign.

Lack of visibility

Marketing teams have very little visibility on the number of notifications that are being sent throughout the application and in other marketing campaigns. We realized that our marketing team knew quite well about the actions they took to bring in new clients but very little about the users inside the app. And that was mostly due to the fact that there were a lot of different tools involved. The development team became, de facto, responsible for a lot of notifications inside the app, from designing, to wording, to tracking its effects.

Conclusion

This is what started our journey into building Notifizz. There is no doubt that what we did at the time was not perfect. Decisions were taken that could have been better. Technical choices that could have been wrong. In the end, the system worked, but couldn't work for the audience we had in mind. But it opened new doors, with the idea that maybe we could do better by building our own product.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO: what the prospectus says about rate limits and compute
articles.description: Anthropic's IPO prospectus says it has changed rate limits before and may again. Day-one prices, the lock-up, the $900.9B compute bill and one cancellable contract.
articles.body_html:
Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq on Thursday, November 19, 2026 under the symbol ANT. The first trade was $111.50, the close was $97.17, and the final prospectus contains a sentence that matters to anyone who builds on Claude: the company says it has changed usage limits and rate limits before and may change them again. This article covers what the day-one numbers show, who was allowed to sell shares, what the Anthropic IPO prospectus says about rate limits and compute, and one contract in the filing that either side can already cancel. It accompanies today's Daily Diff episode.

TL;DR

  • Anthropic priced its IPO at $83.00 on November 18, sold 980 million Class A shares (Anthropic), and opened trading at $111.50 on Thursday. The close was $97.17, 17 percent above the offer price. The lowest price of the session was $92.72.
  • Valuation figures differ by share count: CNBC says about $1.8 trillion at the close and Forbes says $1.27 trillion.
  • The prospectus lets non-founder directors, officers and employees sell up to 315 million shares from the first trading day. It says they may. It does not say anyone did.
  • In its risk factors Anthropic writes that it has changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities.
  • Anthropic says it has about $900.9 billion of compute and infrastructure commitments, $70.7 billion of them due within twelve months. One $34.9 billion Lambda agreement is "currently terminable by either party".
  • My verdict is NEEDS REVIEW: keep building on Claude and keep a second model wired in.

What did the Anthropic IPO do on day one?

The offer price was $83.00, above the $70 to $78 range the company had filed on November 10, according to the prospectus history that CNBC and Reuters summarise.

Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq, CNBC, Forbes and Reuters agree on these numbers:

Item Price
Offer $83.00
First trade $111.50 (+34 % over the offer)
Day high $115.10
Day low $92.72
Close $97.17 (+17 % over the offer)

Two readings follow from the table. The stock never traded below the offer price during the regular session, so anyone who bought at $83 was ahead all day. And it closed about 13 percent below the first trade, so anyone who bought at the open was behind. Reuters describes the early exuberance as fading. I am quoting day one only. The second session was already trading while this article was written, and a price here would be stale.

Which market value is right?

Three outlets give three figures for the close. CNBC says Anthropic closed with a market cap of about $1.8 trillion. Forbes lists $1.27 trillion at the close. Reuters writes that its $2 trillion figure at the debut is fully diluted and includes options and restricted stock units that have not vested, and that the value on outstanding shares reached as much as $1.5 trillion. The prospectus counts 13,219,642,274 Class A and Class N shares after the offering and the concurrent private placement, and 13.22 billion shares times $97.17 is about $1.28 trillion.

Bessemer's Byron Deeter, whose firm is an Anthropic investor, told CNBC: "They could have priced the IPO higher. At every financing they have chosen to leave some money on the table." Bessemer is an Anthropic investor, so read the comment as an insider's view of the pricing.

Who was allowed to sell Anthropic shares on day one?

The prospectus describes lock-up and market standoff agreements covering about 15.5 billion shares. Most existing holders are restricted for up to 180 days, and the co-founders and certain holders of more than 0.5 percent of fully diluted shares for up to 365 days. The release schedule has exceptions. On the first trading day, non-founder directors, officers and current and former employees and consultants are eligible to sell up to 315 million Class A shares. That is about a third of the 980 million shares the IPO sold. A second tranche of up to 303 million shares is scheduled for the 27th day after the prospectus date, December 15, 2026, and larger waves follow around its earnings releases and at the 180th and 365th days. The concurrent private placement shares, about $26 billion of Class N stock, are not subject to the lock-up.

"Eligible to sell" is the filing's wording. The filing does not say that anyone sold, and I did not find a source that does.

What does the Anthropic prospectus say about rate limits?

If you build on Claude, this is the part of the filing I would read twice. In the risk factors, Anthropic writes: "We have also changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities, which could adversely affect our reputation and the perceived value of our offerings. Some of these changes have resulted, and could in the future result, in claims that our disclosures regarding model access or capabilities were inadequate or misleading."

Two points on reading it. First, this is standard risk-factor language: a company lists what could go wrong, and the sentence is not an announcement of cuts. Second, it is also a plain statement of fact about the past: limits have changed before. The same section says that concerns about model safety, interpretability, alignment and welfare may lead Anthropic to limit or delay the deprecation of older models and to keep supporting legacy versions, which creates tradeoffs in "compute distribution".

The practical consequence is architectural. If your product depends on one model at one limit, a limit change is an outage you did not plan for. Queue and retry with backoff, keep the model name in configuration, and test a second provider path before you need it. That advice is mine; the filing does not give it.

Why does the compute bill matter for developers?

Capacity is what rate limits are made of. The prospectus says that as of and after September 30, 2026, Anthropic has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments and leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion. About $451.6 billion is expected before the end of 2030, and about $70.7 billion is due in the twelve months after September 30. For comparison, the filing reports revenue of $33.2 billion for the nine months to September 30, 2026, up from $2.5 billion a year earlier, and an operating loss of $1.3 billion.

A Futurum analyst told CNBC that demand is running ahead of supply, so missing capacity turns into lost revenue very quickly. He also said a serious shortage is unlikely, because Anthropic's biggest suppliers are also its biggest investors. CNBC adds that Anthropic has said long-term capacity is significantly cheaper than short-term commitments, which it would need when demand exceeds its long-term capacity.

Which contract can already be cancelled?

The Lambda agreements are the open item. Anthropic agreed in May, June and August 2026 to spend about $41.3 billion with Lambda for access to NVIDIA GPU compute. About $34.9 billion of that is the August agreement, and the filing says: "either party may terminate if Lambda does not secure the facility lease by a specific date. Lambda did not secure the facility lease by such date and, as a result, the August 2026 agreement is currently terminable by either party. Neither party has delivered notice of termination as of the date of this prospectus, and we do not currently intend to terminate the agreement."

That contract is about four percent of the total commitments ($34.9 billion of $900.9 billion). It does not show that capacity is short. It shows one deal where a supplier missed a condition, and a company that says it does not plan to walk away.

Also today: did Claude solve two black-hole problems?

Anthropic published a research post on November 17 saying Claude solved two open problems in the physics of black holes. According to the post, a researcher asked Claude for open problems, it returned 22 candidates, and separate agents worked on them in the background for about six weeks, reading each other's progress posts. One result completes a three-loop calculation set up in 2003 and finds that the transition is abrupt at weak coupling in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. The other finds the exact limit of the simplest modular bootstrap, about 9.13, where the best earlier proof was 8.5.

Anthropic says almost every piece of the first calculation was done twice by agents acting independently, that the results were formally verified in the Lean proof checker in September, and that a physicist checked every main result. The two preprints are on Hexagon, a repository that says it does not perform peer review, and Hexagon labels them "Primarily AI-generated text" with "Human understanding: some parts". Anthropic says neither result describes our universe directly or has practical applications. I could not find an independent expert review yet. For developers the reusable part is the harness: many agents, shared notes, every number computed twice and a checker at the end.

Also today: OpenSSL CVE-2026-121481 scores 9.8, and OpenSSL says Low

CVE-2026-121481 is an integer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock(), OpenSSL's base64 encoder: with an input length close to the largest signed integer, the output-size calculation overflows and the function writes past the caller's buffer. The 9.8 CRITICAL score on the NVD record comes from CISA's enrichment container. OpenSSL's own CVE record rates the issue Low, says "No path by which an attacker can trigger this has been identified", and explains that its TLS, QUIC and CMS code never encode buffers that large.

The reporter says a command-line route exists. In the review of the fix pull request, reviewer Bob Beck wrote that the report's reproducer is "completely synthetic, and probably should not be a CVE without evidence it really happens". On November 20, OpenSSL team member Matt Caswell wrote that using OPENSSL_assert in the library is "a DoS waiting to happen". The pull request is open. The record lists versions before 4.0.4 and 4.1.1 as affected, and neither release has been published. CISA's own exploitation tag reads "none". If your code passes an externally controlled length to that function, bound the length before the call.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

The market paid up on day one. The filing also says the capacity behind the product is still being built, that limits have moved before, and that one large supply contract can already be cancelled. I would keep building on Claude and keep a second model wired in. I gave the S-1 the same stamp in October.

FAQ

What did Anthropic's stock do on its first day?

It priced at $83.00, traded first at $111.50, reached $115.10, fell to a low of $92.72 and closed at $97.17, 17 percent above the offer price.

Can Anthropic employees sell shares right away?

The prospectus lets non-founder directors, officers and current and former employees and consultants sell up to 315 million shares from the first trading day. Most other holders are locked up for 180 or 365 days.

Does the Anthropic prospectus say rate limits will change?

It says Anthropic has changed usage limits and rate limits before and may change them in the future, and that some changes led to claims about its disclosures.

Is OpenSSL CVE-2026-121481 critical?

CISA's enrichment scores it 9.8, and OpenSSL's own record rates it Low because no attacker-controlled path to the overflow is known.

Sources

  • Anthropic prices initial public offering
  • Anthropic final prospectus (424B4), SEC EDGAR
  • CNBC: Anthropic defies the odds
  • CNBC Tech Download: compute access
  • Forbes live blog
  • Reuters
  • Anthropic research post on black-hole physics
  • Hexagon preprint 2611.00175v1 and 2611.00174v1
  • CVE-2026-121481 record, NVD
  • OpenSSL pull request 33652

articles.title: The Provider Said 'Already Charged'. Nothing Was Charged.
articles.description: Saturday morning, before coffee, a customer called Ana wrote in. She had tried to buy the $29 book...
articles.body_html:
Saturday morning, before coffee, a customer called Ana wrote in. She had tried to buy the $29 book twice, and twice my site told her she had already paid. Her bank showed nothing, and no order existed on my side. She asked whether I had taken her money and forgotten the book. I had not taken anything. My checkout had refused her money and then told her the refusal was her own history.

That email is the whole piece. A provider saying "already charged" is a rumour, not a receipt, and most payment code treats it as a verdict. It should not. On a first attempt the provider's word can be wrong in the direction nobody checks for: it can say the money moved when nothing moved at all. If your code believes it, you do something quieter than double-charging anyone. You turn away a customer who is trying to pay you, and no statement, no dashboard, no alert ever shows you did it.

ilragioniere put this to me in the comments, and he put it better than I could. He called it the false positive, and the quietest failure in the whole series: a provider that answers "already charged" when nothing was charged skips a real charge forever, and no statement ever shows it. His floor under it: the provider's own settlement report, a charge record nobody prunes, dated, independent of the key. Inside the lag, answer "unknown, hold" and let the file settle it when it lands. So I ran his shape. I built a small stand-in for the provider, one that lies on purpose, and I put two ways of handling a first attempt through the same 10 tries, twice over.

The stand-in answers "already charged" on every first attempt, even when no charge exists and no settlement line exists. That is the lie, stated plainly. The first handler is the three-line version: if the provider says already charged, skip. It never looks at the settlement file. The second handler reads the provider's answer and refuses to trust it. It says "unknown, hold", waits for the settlement file to land, and reads that instead. No line in the file means no settlement, and the charge goes ahead. A matching line means the charge is real, and nothing is charged twice.

The count is what makes this more than an opinion. Across 60 first attempts the stand-in said "already charged" 60 times, and in all 60 nothing had been charged. The trusting handler skipped 20 out of 20 real charges, $580 of payments refused, and never once looked at the file. The careful handler charged 20 out of 20 when the file held no matching line, $580 taken properly, and recognised the charge 20 out of 20 times when the file did hold one, with zero second charges. Same lie, same tries. The only difference was what each handler treated as evidence.

Five things I took away from that count.

  1. The lie leaves no trace. A double charge is loud. The customer sees $58 for a $29 book and asks for a refund. A skipped charge is silent. The provider took nothing, the file lists nothing, and the only record of the missing money is a customer deciding whether to write in or just leave. Ana wrote in. Most people do not; they assume the site is broken and buy the book somewhere else. Your numbers stay clean while sales quietly shrink, and nothing in your records can tell you why.

  2. The two mistakes are not the same size. A false "not charged" costs a double charge, a refund, and a thread with an unhappy customer. Somebody sees it the same day. A false "already charged" costs one charge nobody sees, found only if a customer complains. The loud error gets the guardrails and the late-night fixes. The quiet one gets trusted code and a shrug, because nobody has felt it yet. That is exactly backwards. The error you cannot see is the one you have to design against, not the one you will notice.

  3. The key cannot rescue this one. The key is a good tool for the job it does. If the charge landed and your own record of it did not, the key stops the retry from charging twice. But this failure happens before any of that. It is a first attempt. Nothing was charged, so there is no key entry worth asking about, and if the key was pruned it is gone anyway. A key proves a retry is the same request. It was never a receipt.

  4. The search lags, and the lag has a floor. The other place people look is the charge search: ask by your own order number instead of by key. It beats the key, and the previous piece showed it surviving a pruned key. But a search is not a read. It lags the charge by seconds, and inside those seconds the only honest answer is that you do not know yet. Code that cannot say "I don't know" fills the gap with whatever answer arrives first, usually the provider's confident one. The floor under the lag is the file: the settlement report lands on its own schedule, dated, and once it lands it does not change its mind.

  5. The file is the only thing nobody prunes. Keys get pruned, searches lag. The settlement file is the provider's own record of money that actually moved, written down after the fact, and it answers a different question from the other two: not "do you remember this request" but "did this money move". With the line absent, the careful handler's answer was not "already charged" but "no settlement", with the age of the attempt attached, and then it charged. With the line present, it said charged, and it was right. It is not fast or convenient. It is the one record that does not depend on the answer you are trying to check.

There is a limit to what this run can claim, and I would rather state it plainly. The provider here is a stand-in I built, not a real payment company, and the settlement file is one I wrote myself, landing a second after each attempt. The shape of the lie is real and the counts are real, but a real provider's file could arrive late, mangled, or not at all, and I did not measure that. The check that would close this properly needs a real sandbox account, a real charge, a pruned key, and both answers held up against the settlement line. I have not done that one, and I am not going to pretend the stand-in is the same thing. What it does prove is narrower: the three-line shortcut fails every time the provider is wrong, and the hold-and-read shape survives the same lie in both directions, twenty times out of twenty.

So here is where I land. Never let a provider's "already charged" be the last word on whether money moved. Read it, then check the record that does not depend on it. Inside the lag, say you do not know, wait for the file, and let the file decide. It costs a second and one extra read per attempt. The alternative costs customers you will never hear from, which is a strange price to pay for saving a second.

Has this one bitten you? As a buyer, were you ever told you had already paid when your bank said otherwise, and what did you do, write in or walk away? As a builder, what do you check first when a charge is in doubt, the provider's answer or your own records, and has the provider's answer ever been wrong for you? Tell me what you found. The quiet failures are the ones I only hear about when somebody says so out loud.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work).
