articles.title: The Guardrails I Give My AI Coding Agent
articles.description: In my last post I wrote that the more I use AI to code, the more engineering judgment matters. A fair...
articles.body_html:
In my last post I wrote that the more I use AI to code, the more engineering judgment matters. A fair follow-up question is: what does that judgment look like on an ordinary day?

For the past few weeks, an AI coding agent (Claude Code, in my case) has been writing much of the code for our product's search pages. In one day this week it shipped four separate changes to our development environment: a new way to combine filters with a plain-text view of a search, two small visual fixes, and a layout change for smaller laptop screens.

I didn't write those changes. I did decide what got built, what shipped and what "done" meant.

Those decisions are what I want to describe. Most of them are not clever. They are guardrails: rules the agent follows every time, so that speed doesn't turn into surprises.

1. Two decisions stay with me: build it, and ship it

The agent can investigate, propose and build. When it finishes an investigation, it gives me a recommendation rather than a list of every possible option, and then it waits. My answer is usually short: "Yes, build it."

When the change is built and checked, it stops again and asks whether to ship. "Yes, ship it" is a separate decision, and it is mine.

Splitting the two matters more than it sounds. The first approval is about the idea. The second is about the result, after I have seen it. Without the second stop, approving an idea quietly turns into approving whatever came out.

2. Show me, don't tell me

A description of a UI change is not evidence. Every visual change goes onto a local preview first, and the agent sends me screenshots before anything is pushed.

Take the layout change from this week. On a smaller laptop, the panel beside our search form pushed its main buttons, View Results and Download, below the edge of the screen. The fix keeps the count at the top and the buttons at the bottom, and lets only the details between them scroll.

The agent didn't stop at "it works on my screen". It checked:

  • 1366 x 640, a common short laptop window: the buttons end 24 pixels above the bottom edge.
  • 1366 x 560, a very short window: still visible.
  • 1440 x 1000: nothing scrolls, so nothing should look different, and nothing did.
  • Tablet and phone widths, where the page uses a different layout altogether.

At each size it also ran a small script that looks for anything spilling sideways out of its container, the kind of overflow that is easy to miss at a glance.

If you take one habit from this post, take this one: decide which screen sizes count, and make "checked at those sizes, with screenshots" part of done.

3. Merge only on green, and only the commit that was tested

The agent opens a pull request and waits for CI. It merges only when every check is green, and it pins the merge to the exact commit the checks ran against:

gh pr checks "$PR" --watch --fail-fast
gh pr merge "$PR" --merge --match-head-commit "$HEAD_SHA"

--match-head-commit makes the merge fail if anything was pushed to the branch after the checks started. Without it, "CI was green" can describe a different commit from the one that lands.

A red check is never something to talk around. Either the code gets fixed, or the agent explains why the test itself is out of date, changes it in the open and says so in the pull request. It does not quietly loosen a test to get to green.

4. Tests that pin the rules people forget

Some of my favourite tests are almost embarrassingly simple. They read a source file as text and check it with a regular expression:

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import fs from 'node:fs';

const css = fs.readFileSync('resources/css/search.css', 'utf8');

test('colours come from design tokens, never hex values', () => {
  assert.doesNotMatch(css, /#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b/);
});

A test like this caught the agent this week. To fade the edges of the new scrolling area, it used a CSS mask with #000 in the gradient. The colour never even shows (a mask only uses transparency), but the rule is the rule, and the test failed. The fix took seconds: black instead of #000. What matters is that I didn't have to notice it.

We have tests like this for:

  • no em dashes or curly quotes in customer-facing text (a single curly apostrophe in a release note failed the tests once, which is exactly what I wanted);
  • a maximum length for release note titles and summaries;
  • a line limit on one large component, which pushes new logic into its own file instead of growing one file forever.

None of these rules are hard to check. They are hard to remember, especially at the speed an agent works. A rule that lives only in a style guide will be broken eventually. A rule that lives in a test is checked every time.

5. Every change ships with its own story

Each user-facing change includes two pieces of writing in the same pull request:

  • a short "What's New" entry that customers see in the product, with a title under 70 characters and a summary under 260;
  • a line in our internal product document saying what changed, why, who asked for it and where the code lives.

The agent writes both. It knows the change better than anyone at that moment, so this is the cheapest time to write it down. Because it happens in the same pull request, the documentation never falls a release behind, and tests hold the customer-facing text to its length and style limits.

6. Check it where it lives, and leave it as you found it

Green CI and a good local preview are not the end. After each deploy, the agent opens the change on our development environment and checks it again, using my own saved search as the test case.

That comes with firm limits:

  • It never touches production.
  • It never signs in as me. If the session has expired, it tells me and waits.
  • On the development environment it reads, and avoids changing real records or running expensive exports.
  • When it has to change something to test it, such as a draft search, it saves the original first and puts it back afterwards.

The last point matters more than it seems. A test environment that slowly fills up with leftovers from automated checks stops being trustworthy.

7. Write the traps down

Every project has traps that cost an afternoon the first time. The agent keeps a notes file of them and reads it at the start of every session.

One example from our search: when the agent set up a test search using a field's internal sample name instead of its real name, the filter still appeared on screen, but the search silently ignored it. The count looked plausible and was wrong. That trap is now one line in the notes, with the rule that goes with it: always use the live field name.

The format doesn't matter much. What matters is that a lesson learned once isn't paid for again in the next session.

8. Small, boring commits

A few habits keep the history easy to read and easy to undo:

  • One change per pull request, even on a day with four of them.
  • Files are staged by name, never with a blanket git add, so scratch files and stray experiments don't ride along.
  • Commit messages say what changed for the user, not only what changed in the code.

If something goes wrong, I want to point at one small pull request and revert it without unpicking three other things.

What the guardrails are really for

None of this slows the agent down much. Most of it is automated, and the rest is two short answers from me. What it changes is what I am responsible for.

I don't need to read every line at the speed it was written. I need to be confident about the things that matter: what the change does, that it was tested at the sizes and in the situations we care about, that it follows our rules, and that what was tested is what shipped. The guardrails turn those from things I hope are true into things that are checked.

In my last post I said that if I ship something, I need to be able to explain it, debug it and maintain it. These guardrails are a large part of how I keep that promise while an agent does most of the typing.

What guardrails have you put around AI-written code? I'd especially like to hear about cheap checks that have caught real mistakes.

articles.title: I Built a Claude Code Plugin Because I Was Becoming a Rubber-Stamp Reviewer
articles.description: My development team has two members: me and AI. And lately, I've been feeling like I'm becoming the...
articles.body_html:
My development team has two members: me and AI. And lately, I've been feeling like I'm becoming the less useful member of the team.

I've been using AI coding agents for years. Claude Code, and plenty of other tools. They're incredible at what they do, but somewhere along the way, my development process started looking like this:

Me: "Implement this feature."

AI: "Done! Changed 27 files, added 3,400 lines, refactored two modules. All tests passed."

Me: "LGTM."

Narrator: He did not, in fact, look.

The code gets written. Features get shipped. Productivity looks great. But here's what bothers me: Am I actually reviewing the code anymore, or am I just approving whatever the AI tells me?

And if I'm not making the technical decisions, what exactly is my role as a developer?

The problem isn't that AI writes code

I don't think developers need to manually write every line of code. That's not the point. The problem is that we're slowly outsourcing something much more important than typing: our judgment.

Think about how often this happens. The AI makes an architectural decision without asking you. It assumes a requirement that was never specified. It changes something outside the original scope. Then it confidently reports that all tests passed, and you trust the summary because reviewing everything yourself would take too long.

None of this necessarily means the AI is bad at coding. It means our development workflow hasn't caught up with how much code AI can produce.

I wanted a workflow where AI could do most of the implementation without quietly taking ownership of the decisions. I also didn't want to become an unpaid project manager, manually breaking everything into tiny tasks and supervising every step.

So I built human-rights.


GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

human-rights is an open-source Claude Code plugin built around a simple idea: Don't make humans review every line. Make sure they understand and approve the decisions that matter.

The requirements. The architecture. The risks. The acceptance criteria. And the evidence that the implementation actually works.

But there's an obvious problem with this approach. If every tiny change requires a design document, three approvals, and a meeting with yourself, nobody is going to use it.

So the workflow adapts to the task.

  1. Not every change deserves the same process

human-rights classifies development requests into four levels, from simple edits to high-risk changes.

Level

Example

Workflow

L0 — Direct

Center a login card

Make the change and check it

L1 — Focused

Add input validation hints

Short plan and targeted tests

L2 — Planned

Add Google authentication

Investigate, design, and review

L3 — Governed

Modify safety-critical control logic

Human approvals, integration tests, and final verification

The classification considers ambiguity, scope, architectural impact, risk, verification difficulty, and dependencies. A small UI change shouldn't require the same process as modifying authentication or controlling physical hardware.

For larger changes, the agent investigates the existing code, asks questions that could change the design, and creates a testable implementation plan. If the request is too large, it first breaks the work into smaller features that can be reviewed and verified independently.

The human decides what should happen. The AI figures out how to implement it.

  1. The AI cannot simply approve its own work

This was one of the most important design decisions. I didn't want to rely entirely on instructions like "Always ask the user for approval." An AI agent following a prompt is not the same thing as an enforced workflow.

So human-rights has two parts: a Claude Code skill that decides what process a task needs, and a deterministic Python runtime that enforces state transitions, approvals, test evidence, and failure handling.

Design approvals are tied to the approved plan, while final approvals are tied to the code being verified. If the plan changes, the previous design approval becomes invalid. If the code changes, the final approval becomes invalid too.

A test result is not accepted just because the agent says it passed. The runtime records the execution result and associates it with the relevant code version.

The goal is simple: stop trusting the AI's description of what happened and start requiring evidence of what actually happened.

  1. Then I realized something worse: humans can still blindly approve everything

Even with all those safeguards, there's a fundamental weakness in the system.

The human.

You can build the most carefully controlled approval system in the world, and I can still click "Approve" without reading anything.

So I added a feature called Red Pill Mode.

Here's how it works. When enabled, the system occasionally introduces a deliberately incorrect item into the review material. The developer is supposed to notice it before approving the work.

For example, suppose the original requirement says:

The system must support four simultaneous drone connections.

But the review table contains:

TEST-010: Verify that two simultaneous drone connections work correctly.

Would you notice the difference? Or would you just approve?

If you catch the incorrect item, the system records the catch and explains why it was wrong. If you blindly approve, the approval is blocked.

And yes, it makes fun of you:

You didn't really review this, did you, human? Keep approving like that and the AI really will take your job. lol.

It's intentionally a little ridiculous, but the underlying problem is serious. An approval button means nothing if the person clicking it isn't paying attention.

The planted mistakes never modify the actual implementation plan or executable code. They exist only in the review material, so they cannot accidentally become part of the software being built.

Red Pill Mode is optional and off by default. It also supports adaptive difficulty, so the review exercises can become harder as you successfully identify mistakes.

I find this particularly interesting because we're entering a world where developers may spend more time reviewing AI-generated work than writing code themselves. If that's where we're heading, shouldn't we be actively improving our review skills instead of letting them deteriorate?

  1. Bigger requests are split before implementation

Another issue I kept encountering was asking an agent to implement something too large. It would produce an enormous plan, and I'd be expected to approve the whole thing.

That's not meaningful review. That's just outsourcing a massive amount of work and hoping the result is correct.

So compound requests are split into independently verifiable features. The human approves the feature list before implementation starts, and each feature gets its own workflow, decisions, and verification.

After those features are implemented, the system checks that they work together. Independent tasks can also run in parallel using isolated Git worktrees, while conflicting tasks are kept sequential.

The idea isn't to slow down AI development. It's to gain the speed of AI agents without giving up control of the overall design.

  1. You can try it

The project is currently at v0.5.0 and is open source under the MIT license. It runs as a Claude Code plugin with a Python 3.8+ standard-library runtime.

Install it in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add kiduki77/human-rights

/plugin install hrs@human-rights

Initialize it in your project:

/hrs:init

Then start a task:

/hrs:new add Google authentication

Or, if you want to see whether you're actually paying attention during reviews, try:

/hrs:redpill on 5 adaptive

The repository includes an automated test suite, but this is still an early-stage project. Some integrations, including live GitHub adapter operation and real concurrent sub-agent execution, still need field validation.

GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

Where this could go

Right now, human-rights focuses on individual development workflows, but I think the underlying problem could become much more important for engineering teams.

As AI generates more code, how do we know that code was meaningfully reviewed? How do we distinguish a real technical decision from a rubber-stamp approval? And how do we help developers improve at finding problems instead of gradually losing that skill?

Imagine an engineering team where AI generates most of the code. A developer approves a pull request without noticing that an important requirement was missed. Another developer catches the same issue immediately.

Today, we can track who approved a pull request, but that doesn't necessarily tell us how thoroughly it was reviewed. What if we could help developers identify the types of mistakes they tend to miss, practice reviewing realistic changes, and improve over time?

I think there's an opportunity to build something that doesn't just manage AI-generated code, but helps humans become better reviewers of it.

That's a longer-term idea, not something I'm claiming the current plugin already solves.

For now, I'm starting with the problem I experience every day: making sure I still understand and control the software I'm building.

I'd love to hear what other developers think

I'm especially curious whether other developers have noticed themselves reviewing AI-generated code less carefully over time. Would enforced approval gates help, or would they just become another form of bureaucracy? And would you actually enable something like Red Pill Mode in your own development workflow?

I don't have all the answers, and I'm sure there are things I've overlooked. That's why I'm releasing this as open source and looking for feedback from developers who are experiencing the same problems.

I built this because I don't want to stop using AI.

I just don't want to stop being a developer while using it.

human-rights — AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

articles.title: rm -rf and the Sound It Makes
articles.description: The folder is empty.  Not broken. Not corrupted, not locked, not asking for a password I forgot....
articles.body_html:
The folder is empty.

Not broken. Not corrupted, not locked, not asking for a password I forgot. Empty. The name is still there on the screen, "client-portal", sitting in the list exactly where it always sat, and when I open it there is nothing inside. White space. A scrollbar that has nothing to scroll. I stare at it for a long time, the way you stare at a room after someone has moved out of it and taken everything, even the smell.

I know what I did. That is the worst part. There was no crash, no power cut, no mysterious bug to blame. I typed it. I watched it run. I pressed enter like a man posting a letter.

Three weeks of work. A client portal, the whole thing: login, dashboard, the invoice list, the file upload that took me four days because the progress bar lied and I believed it. Gone in the time it takes to blink. The command does not ask twice. It does not say "are you sure" in the tone of a friend. It just does what you told it to do, and then it waits, politely, for your next instruction, as if nothing happened.

That is the sound it makes. Nothing. No error, no warning, no sad trombone. Just the cursor, blinking, on a fresh empty line.

Forty minutes earlier I am sitting at the same desk, and the folder is full, and I am annoyed at it.

The annoyance is specific. There is a folder inside the project called "client-portal-old" and another one called "client-portal-backup", and a third one called "client-portal-final", and none of them are what their names say they are. The "final" one is from two weeks ago. The "backup" one has half the files. The "old" one is somehow newer than the "final" one. I have been meaning to clean this up for days. Today is the day. I will delete the old ones, keep the real one, and stop living like this.

I open the terminal. I type the command the way I have typed it a hundred times. The folder name after it. I check it. I check it again, because I am the kind of person who checks. The name looks right. The path looks right. I press enter.

The screen does what screens do. A line of output, gone too fast to read. And then nothing.

I do not notice at first. I notice when I look for the folder and it is not where I left it. Not the old one. The real one. The one with three weeks in it. My eyes do the thing eyes do when the brain has not caught up yet: they scan the list again, slower, as if the folder is hiding behind another folder, as if it will step out and say it was a joke.

It does not step out.

Three hours earlier, the folder is full, and I am proud of it, and that is what makes the whole thing worse.

I had just finished the file upload. Four days on a progress bar. Four days because the bar would climb to ninety percent and stop, and I would sit there watching it the way you watch a kettle, and then I found it: the thing was reporting the wrong total. It was measuring the wrong file. One line. One wrong variable, and the bar had been lying to me for a week. I fixed it in eleven minutes and sat there laughing at my own screen, alone, at my desk, because the fix was so small and the days were so long.

I showed it to a friend on a call. He watched a file climb from zero to a hundred in a straight honest line and said "nice", which is the highest praise a developer ever gives another developer. I closed the call feeling like a person who knows what he is doing. I wrote a commit message that said "upload progress fixed, finally". I meant the "finally" in the warm way. The way you say it when a thing is done.

That commit is gone too. Everything is gone. The fix, the message, the "finally". The whole three weeks, and the feeling that went with it.

The morning of the same day, the folder is full, and I am building the invoice list, and I am thinking about the name of the project.

"Client-portal" is a boring name. I know it is a boring name. I named it on the first day, in a hurry, because the folder needed a name before it needed anything else, and I never renamed it. Every project I have ever made has a boring first-day name that stuck. There is a folder on this machine called "test-final" that holds a whole website. There is one called "new-app-2" that holds the thing I am proudest of. I tell myself I will rename them one day, when there is time, and there is never time, and the names stay, and after a while the boring name starts to feel like the real name, the way a nickname you hate at first becomes the only thing anyone calls you.

I am building the invoice list and thinking about this, and about how the list needs to show the paid ones in green and the overdue ones in red, and how the red ones should not shout, just sit there quietly, because nobody likes being shouted at by an invoice. Small decisions. The kind that take ten seconds and shape the whole thing. I make about forty of them before lunch and forget thirty-nine.

A week before that, the folder is nearly empty, and I am starting.

Starting is the part nobody talks about. The first file. The blank page with a cursor on it, waiting. I sit there for twenty minutes doing nothing that looks like work: moving the window, checking the time, opening the folder and closing it again. Then I write the first line. It is a bad line. I know it is a bad line even as I write it. But it is a line, and a line is a beginning, and a beginning is the only thing a blank folder cannot give you.

By the end of the first day there are six files. By the end of the first week there are thirty. I do not remember writing most of them. I remember the stuck moments, the afternoons when nothing worked and I walked around the room and came back and it worked, and I remember the small wins, the button that finally lined up, the page that loaded in under a second. The rest is a blur, the way a road trip is a blur except for the wrong turns and the good meals.

Three weeks. Thirty-something files. One wrong command.

The folder is empty.

I sit there for a while, and then I do the only thing there is to do. I open a new folder with the same boring name, and I start again.

The second version is better. I know that sounds like the kind of thing people say to make themselves feel better, and maybe it is, but it is also true. The first version's mistakes are the one thing I remember perfectly. I remember every place I got stuck, every wrong turn, every line I wrote and then wrote around instead of fixing. This time I do not write around them. I fix them. The upload bar works on the first try. The invoice list takes an afternoon instead of two days. The login page, which took me a week the first time because I kept second-guessing it, takes a morning.

It is not faster because I am smarter. It is faster because the first version taught me where the walls are, and this time I walk around them instead of into them.

By the end of the week the folder is full again. Fuller than before, in fewer files, with fewer apologies hidden in the comments. I show it to the same friend on the same kind of call. The file climbs from zero to a hundred in a straight honest line. He says "nice". I do not tell him it is the second time he has seen it. Nobody ever knows. The client never knows. The portal ships on time, and it works, and the first version, the one with the "finally" in its commit message, never existed as far as anyone can tell.

Sometimes I open the folder just to look at it. Not to change anything. Just to see that it is full. And then I close it, and I check the path twice before I type anything, and I always will now.

The command still does not ask twice. I am the one who asks twice. Every time.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: How I built Reserve: an agent that refuses to trade
articles.description: Building a tokenized-stock agent on Base where the guard, not the agent, decides whether money...
articles.body_html:
Building a tokenized-stock agent on Base where the guard, not the agent, decides whether money moves.

The problem, stated plainly

A trading agent on Base is a loop: read price, decide, send tx. Every failure mode hides in "read price."

A ticker paused for a split still returns a price. A Chainlink feed outside 24/5 hours still returns a price — yesterday's. An agent that trusts those numbers will happily buy at the wrong one, and nobody finds out until settlement.

Reserve inverts the default. Money never moves because the agent decided. It moves because a separate contract agreed.

Three contracts, one seam

  • ReserveVault — holds USDC and the tokenized stock, keeps the book, exposes execute(action, asset, amount).
  • Guard — pure policy. Takes an intent, returns bytes32 — zero for OK, or a reason hash like FEED_STALE.
  • IMarketData — a three-value view: (multiplierWad, pending, effectiveAt).

That third one is the whole portability trick. Testnet and mainnet read completely different infrastructure, but the shape the Guard sees is identical, so Guard.sol and ReserveVault.sol compile to the same bytecode on both chains. Only the adapter swaps: mocks on Sepolia, Chainlink + Coinbase's onchain registry on mainnet.

The multiplier matters more than it looks. B20 tokenized stocks don't rebase — a dividend or split arrives as a multiplier that changes your displayed balance while balanceOf stays put. There's a window where the registry has announced the multiplier but hasn't applied it. Pricing a trade inside that window is pricing a number that's about to change.

Refusal as a state machine

Four checks, all before any transfer:

  1. pausedFeatures() non-empty → PAUSED_CORPORATE_ACTION
  2. multiplier announced, not yet effective → MULTIPLIER_PENDING
  3. feed timestamp older than its heartbeat → FEED_STALE
  4. post-trade liquid balance under the operating floor → RESERVE_FLOOR_BREACH

One rule outranks all of them: repay is always allowed. A guard that blocks de-risking is worse than no guard.

And refusals are not exceptions — they're transactions. The agent submits them onchain and the contract emits an event with the reason hash. Which produces the demo's central number: 17 intents, 14 refusals, 3 settlements.

A refusal you can only find in a log file isn't auditable; one that's a tx with a block number is. That's the design decision I'd defend hardest. It would have been cheaper to return early offchain and log to a JSON file. It would also have meant the product's main claim — that the no is verifiable — was a screenshot.

The agent

A viem loop, ~120 lines. Each cycle: read the book, propose an intent, ask the Guard, submit either way, append the receipt to runs.jsonl. Nothing clever. The interesting part is that the loop never decides whether to trade safely — it decides what it wants, and the Guard decides whether it's allowed.

I hit a real bug here that's worth naming: the intent amount is 8-decimal USD, the vault transfer is 6-decimal USDC. For a while the loop was passing 2e8 into a token call expecting 2e6 — a 100× error that looked like a book imbalance. Fixed by keeping two constants and never letting them meet.

Paying for its own data

The risk verdict is also sold over x402. GET /verdict/:asset returns 402 with a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header, the agent signs an exact-EVM USDC transfer, retries, gets 200 with a PAYMENT-RESPONSE receipt. Settled for $0.001 — real tx, block 60921570.

The satisfying detail: the verdict it buys back is safe: false, FEED_STALE. The oracle sells refusals, not prices. That's the product in one response.

// seller, x402 v2
const server = new x402ResourceServer(new HTTPFacilitatorClient(...))
  .register("eip155:84532", new ExactEvmScheme());

app.use(paymentMiddleware({
  "GET /verdict/:asset": { price: "$0.001", network: "eip155:84532" }
}, server));

The dashboard is a build artifact

Base's public Sepolia RPC caps eth_getLogs at 200 blocks, and the ledger spans thousands. So scripts/snapshot.mjs doesn't query logs at all — it walks the tx hashes from runs.jsonl plus a hand-maintained list, fetches each receipt, and classifies by topic. Output is a static state.json that the page renders with no client-side RPC.

Ugly, and correct. It also means the dashboard can't lie about live state: if the snapshot script fails, the page shows old numbers rather than inventing new ones.

What's faked, on purpose

Sepolia has no B20 ticker — Coinbase's /chains endpoint lists exactly one chain, 8453, and the mainnet registry contracts have zero code on 84532. So the stock and the price feed are mocks. That's disclosed in the README, on the dashboard, and in the video. The Guard and the vault aren't mocked, which is the part being judged.

18 Foundry tests, 5 of them running against live Base mainnet state.

What I'd do next

The borrow leg. Supplying stock as collateral and refusing to borrow when a corporate action starts mid-position is where the refusal model stops being a demo and starts being infrastructure.

Live: https://reserve-book.vercel.app
Code: https://github.com/harishkotra/reserve

articles.title: Stop Trimming Tool Descriptions. They Were Never the Biggest Part.
articles.description: kevinhall left a comment on my piece about the 200-tool menu, and it pointed at the one split my run...
articles.body_html:
kevinhall left a comment on my piece about the 200-tool menu, and it pointed at the one split my run never made. He had measured real hosted tools, and the heaviest definition he found was almost all an output schema the server had made up from past runs, nothing the author wrote. So the cost was not always in the descriptions. My run never split the output schema out from the description and the input schema, so I could not say whether he was right, or how far it went.

I split five real server definitions open this week: the filesystem, memory, sequential-thinking, everything, and github servers, 68 tools in total, counted the same way as the earlier runs so the totals reproduce exactly. The answer is messier than either of us expected. kevinhall is right that the cost is not in the descriptions. He is wrong about where it is. And the split turned up something neither of us was looking for, hiding in the heaviest server of all.

My claim before the numbers: the output schema would be the biggest chunk on the heavy servers, and trimming descriptions would be trimming the wrong thing. The first half was wrong. The second half was right for the wrong reason.

Problem 1: the description is the biggest chunk on none of the five servers

Across all 68 tools, 23,298 tokens of definition: descriptions are 2,619 tokens, 11.2 percent. Input schemas are 6,876, 29.5 percent. Output schemas are 2,205, 9.5 percent. The description is not the largest part anywhere.

On the filesystem server, the input schema is 39.4 percent, the description 26.1, the output schema 18.1. On sequential-thinking, the input schema is 43.8 percent against a 33.8 percent description. On github, the input schema is 84.4 percent and the description is 8.0. And github has no output schema at all, on any of its 26 tools. Stripping every description on all five servers saves 2,619 tokens. The output schema alone is 2,205, nearly as big as all the descriptions put together, and the input schema is nearly three times the descriptions.

So the advice to trim descriptions is trimming the third-biggest bucket at best. It is not useless. 11 percent is 11 percent, and over forty turns it compounds. But it is not where the cost lives, and anyone selling description-trimming as the fix for definition bloat is selling a haircut for a weight problem.

Problem 2: the output schema wins on exactly one server, by 27 tokens

The memory server is the one place kevinhall's shape shows up. Its output schema is 37.3 percent, edging out its input schema at 36.4 percent, and the description is a distant third at 14.2. Stripping every description there saves 453 tokens while the output schema alone costs 1,186, two and a half times more. The three read tools, read_graph, search_nodes and open_nodes, each carry the fattest output schema in the whole set at 238 tokens: the full entity and relation shape, with per-field descriptions.

But here is the detail that changes the story. I checked the shipped server source instead of guessing, and every output schema in this set is author-written. The memory server's schemas are Zod objects written in the server's own code, reusing the same entity shape as the input schema. The filesystem server's output schema is a generic wrapper the author wrote once: {content: string}, the identical 40-token schema on fifteen of its sixteen tools, because the server returns every result as one text blob. The "everything" server's two output schemas are plain JSON Schema literals written by hand. None of them was generated from past runs. None of them describes anything the tool actually returns in particular. The filesystem one does not even try: it is a wrapper that says "the result is text", forty tokens, fifteen times over.

So kevinhall's "made up from past runs" shape does not appear on these five servers. That does not disprove his measurement. His server was a hosted one he did not name, and I could not measure it. It means the pattern is not universal. Whether an output schema dominates depends on whether the server author bothered to write one, and how rich it is. On github, the author did not bother at all. On memory, the author wrote a rich one. The cost follows the author's habits, not the protocol.

Problem 3: the heaviest server is fat with pictures

The surprise came from the heaviest server in the set. The everything test server totals 11,914 tokens across 16 tools, and 9,520 of those, 79.9 percent, are icons. Every one of its tools carries two base64-encoded SVG icons, light and dark, 595 tokens each. The single heaviest tool in the whole set, get-header-params at 898 tokens, is 595 tokens of icons, 108 of input schema, 91 of output schema, and 58 of description. The earlier run called that tool fat on schema richness. The split shows it is mostly pictures.

Strip the icons and the whole test server falls to 2,394 tokens — cheaper than the filesystem server. Whether a host even sends icons to the model is host-dependent, but they are in the listed definition, so they are in the count. And everything is a test server, so its numbers are real but not representative. It is included because it proves the point the other four servers only suggest: schema and icon richness dominates tool count. A server with 16 tools can cost more than a server with 26, because the cost was never about how many tools there are. It is about what each definition carries.

Problem 4: presence is an author choice, not a protocol fact

Step back and the pattern across all five servers is simple. 28 of 68 tools have an output schema. Github has none. The filesystem server's is a 40-token boilerplate repeated fifteen times. The memory server's is a hand-shaped entity graph. Any claim of the form "output schemas cost X percent" needs the server named alongside it, because the answer is 37 percent on one server, 18 on another, 1.4 on a third, and zero on a fourth. There is no general number. There is only the server in front of you, split open.

That is the rule I am keeping, and it is narrower than the one I went in with. Split the definition before you trim anything, because the biggest chunk is different on every server, and on most of them it is the input schema, and on one of them it is pictures. The description is never the biggest chunk. Trim it if you like. 11 percent is real money over forty turns. But trim it knowing it is the third thing on the list, not the first.

The honest limit, stated plainly: these are local stdio servers, not hosted ones. kevinhall measured a real hosted server and did not name it, so I could not re-measure his server. A hosted server that synthesises output schemas from past runs would show a much larger output-schema share than anything here. This run neither confirms nor refutes that shape. It says what the five real official servers actually carry, and what they carry is input schemas, author-written output schemas, and, on the fattest one, pictures.

Have you ever split one of your own tool definitions open? I would like to hear what the fattest part turned out to be, and whether it was the part you expected.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: How a web page can measure your mouse's polling rate
articles.description: Gaming mice advertise 1000, 4000, even 8000 Hz: how often the mouse reports its position to the PC....
articles.body_html:
Gaming mice advertise 1000, 4000, even 8000 Hz: how often the mouse reports its position to the PC. But is yours actually running at that rate? A wireless mode, a setting in the mouse software or a cheap receiver can quietly drop it to 125 Hz.

I wanted a test that runs in the browser, with nothing to download. It turned out to be a nice tour of the Pointer Events API. Here's how it works.

1. Get every report, not every frame

The obvious approach is pointermove. The problem: browsers don't fire one pointermove per mouse report. They bundle all the moves since the last frame into one event, so you'd measure your screen's refresh rate, not your mouse.

Two APIs get around that:

  • pointerrawupdate (Chrome and Edge) fires for every raw report without waiting for the next frame. It only exists on HTTPS pages.
  • getCoalescedEvents() returns the individual events that were bundled into one. 
const raw = 'onpointerrawupdate' in window;

function handle(e) {
  if (e.pointerType !== 'mouse') return;   // fingers and pens have no polling rate
  const list = e.getCoalescedEvents ? e.getCoalescedEvents() : [];
  if (list.length) list.forEach((c) => report(c.timeStamp));
  else report(e.timeStamp);                // fallback: one event per frame, not exact
}

window.addEventListener(raw ? 'pointerrawupdate' : 'pointermove', handle, { passive: true });

It uses the event's own timeStamp, not performance.now(). The timestamp says when the browser received the report; performance.now() would say when the code got around to it, which can be later.

The listener sits on window, so the whole page is the measuring area. The first version used a box on the page, and fast, wide movements kept leaving it.

2. Count reports instead of timing intervals

The natural idea is to time the gap between two reports: 1 ms means 1000 Hz. That breaks at high rates, because browsers round timestamps (a Spectre mitigation). At 8000 Hz reports are 0.125 ms apart, about the size of the rounding step or smaller, so single gaps are meaningless.

Counting is robust: how many reports arrived in the last 500 ms? Rounding only affects the first and the last timestamp, so the error stays tiny.

const WINDOW = 500; // ms of continuous movement per reading
const GAP = 60;     // no report for 60 ms = the mouse stopped
let times = [], last = 0;

function report(t) {
  if (last && t - last > GAP) times = [];   // a pause: start a new window
  last = t;
  times.push(t);
  while (times.length && t - times[0] > WINDOW) times.shift();
}

function rate() {
  const span = times[times.length - 1] - times[0];
  return ((times.length - 1) / span) * 1000;  // reports per second
}

3. A mouse only reports while it moves

This is the part that's easy to get wrong. The polling rate is a maximum: the mouse only sends a report when something changed. Move it slowly and a 1000 Hz mouse may report 300 times a second. Stop, and it reports nothing.

So the test:

  • starts a new window after a 60 ms pause, so pauses don't count as "slow",
  • only shows a reading with 20+ reports spread over at least 400 ms of continuous movement,
  • keeps the best steady reading, because nobody moves a mouse perfectly evenly.

Then it snaps the value to the nearest standard rate when it's within 10 %:

const RATES = [125, 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000];
const snap = (hz) => {
  for (const r of RATES) if (Math.abs(hz - r) / r < 0.1) return r;
  return Math.round(hz / 10) * 10;
};

4. Don't update the page 8000 times a second

At 8000 Hz, touching the DOM in the event handler would cost more than the measurement is worth. The handler only records timestamps; a requestAnimationFrame loop reads the result and updates the numbers at most five times a second.

let shown = 0;

function tick() {
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  const now = performance.now();
  if (now - shown < 200) return;
  if (times.length < 20 || times[times.length - 1] - times[0] < WINDOW * 0.8) return;
  shown = now;
  // snap(rate()), keep the peak, update the text and the graph
}
requestAnimationFrame(tick);

Limits

  • Only Chrome and Edge have pointerrawupdate. Elsewhere it depends on whether getCoalescedEvents() hands over every report. If the browser only delivers one move per frame, the test says so instead of showing a wrong number.
  • At 4000 or 8000 Hz the browser itself can become the bottleneck. If the test shows less than your mouse software, trust the software.
  • No server involved: the timestamps never leave the page.

Try it

The test is live here: Mouse polling rate test. Move the mouse fast, in circles, anywhere on the page. The test itself runs entirely in your browser.

If you get a surprising result, especially on a 4K or 8K mouse, tell me in the comments. I'm curious how browsers behave at the top end.

articles.title: What I learned building 700+ browser-only tools (no uploads, ever)
articles.description: I run theomnikit.com, a free site with 700+ small tools: PDF, image, video, developer utilities and...
articles.body_html:
I run theomnikit.com, a free site with 700+ small tools: PDF, image, video, developer utilities and calculators. Every file tool runs in the visitor's browser. Nothing is uploaded, and that one rule decided most of the engineering.

This is what I learned getting there, including the parts that broke. I wrote this with AI help and checked every claim against the code and the project's decision log.

The rule, and how it is enforced

The first architecture decision was "browser-only; any server-side processing needs a new decision". A rule in a doc is easy to break quietly, so it is enforced by a test:

  • no API route accepts a file (no multipart parser, no upload interceptor);
  • nginx refuses any request body over 1 MB;
  • the API's JSON parser stops at 1 MB.

There is exactly one exception, and it has its own written decision: a screenshot attached to a bug report, redrawn on a canvas into a JPEG of at most 600 KB, so camera and location metadata never leave the device.

One thing I got wrong early: I listed OCR as "out of scope" because I assumed it needed a server. It was the upload I had ruled out, not the reading of text. Image to Text now runs tesseract.js as WebAssembly. Because the CSP is connect-src 'self' and every Tesseract default points at a CDN, the worker, cores and language files are served from our own domain.

How a file tool actually works

The flow is the same everywhere: the File API hands over the bytes, the format is detected from the bytes (not the extension), the heavy library is fetched as soon as the file arrives, and the job runs when the person taps one button that names the action.

Long jobs go to a Web Worker. The PDF tools, such as Grayscale PDF, share a small runner: one worker per tool, created on first use, the ArrayBuffer transferred rather than copied, progress posted back, and a fallback to the main thread when a worker cannot start.

Workers are also a safety valve. The Regex Tester builds its worker from the same function the unit tests cover, and terminates it after 2 seconds, because a pattern that needs longer is almost always backtracking catastrophically.

But a worker is not a fix for a bad algorithm. The diff checker froze on large inputs; moving it to a worker would have stopped the freeze and still failed the same comparisons. It got a better alignment algorithm with a time budget instead.

Video without ffmpeg.wasm

Video was where browser-only nearly broke. Single-threaded ffmpeg.wasm re-encoded a 5-minute 1080p video in 35 to 90 minutes. The multithreaded build needs SharedArrayBuffer, which means COOP/COEP headers, which blank out third-party ads, so that was not an option for a free site.

The video tools, like Trim Video, use WebCodecs with mp4box and mp4-muxer instead: about 50 KB gzipped against ffmpeg's 32 MB. Trimming copies the original frames when the shape stays the same, so a short clip finishes in under a second with no quality loss.

The pitfalls nobody warns you about

iOS Safari's canvas limit. Safari refuses a canvas over about 16.7 megapixels, and recent iPhones shoot 24 MP by default. The failure is not even consistent: sometimes no context, sometimes an InvalidStateError on encode. Image to PDF now caps every encode at 16.7 MP, retries at half the pixels down to 2 MP, and tries a DOM canvas when OffscreenCanvas refuses.

Thumbnails are full photos. Forty 12 MP photos in a preview strip is about 2 GB of decoded pixels on a phone. Thumbnails are now 480 px JPEGs made when the file is added.

HEIC. One image tool accepted HEIC and handed it straight to createImageBitmap, so every HEIC failed in Chrome and Firefox, which cannot decode it. The image tools now share one loader that handles HEIC, and HEIC to JPG decodes with a dedicated library in the browser.

Memory on big files. Before decoding an image, a pixel guard reads width and height from the first 256 KB and refuses an oversized image with a clear message. Running out of memory is reported as "too large for this browser", never as "damaged file", because it says nothing about the file. PDF limits, such as on Compress PDF, were deliberately not raised until browser memory is actually measured.

Feature probes that lie. Every "to WebP" page once told visitors their browser could not write WebP, in a browser that could. The probe encoded a 1x1 OffscreenCanvas that had never had a rendering context, and that throws for every format. Test the probe, not just the feature.

Why every tool is its own page

Each tool has its own URL, title, short answer at the top and structured data, because the site has no marketing budget: people arrive from search engines and AI assistants asking one specific question, and the page has to be the answer.

That also has a limit. Of 151 landing variants Google left "discovered, not indexed", 108 were folded into their parent with a 301. One page per real search intent, not one per keyword.

State lives in the URL too. When one tool suggests the next step (say, compress the PDF you just made), the plan travels as link parameters, and the file is handed over in memory. No account, no server-side history.

The standard that ties it together

The bar for a file tool is two taps on a phone: choose the file, confirm. Zero scrolls. The site never runs a job on a dropped file by itself; that one confirmation is what makes "your files never leave your device" believable.

If you are building something similar: write the no-upload rule down, enforce it with a test, put long jobs in workers, and test on a real iPhone early. Most of my bugs were in that last one.

articles.title: Intl.Locale info: the browser knows your week
articles.description: getWeekInfo(), getHourCycles() and friends tell you the first day of the week, the weekend, 12 or 24 hours and text direction for any locale, with no library.
articles.body_html:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

Your date picker may well start the week on the wrong day for a lot of your users. Since July 2026 every major browser can tell you the right one: new Intl.Locale("he-IL").getWeekInfo() returns { firstDay: 7, weekend: [5, 6] }. That is Intl Locale Info, now Baseline, and it removes a whole category of hardcoded tables.

Pick a few locales in the demo above. The calendar reflows to start on the locale's first day, the weekend columns move, the clock switches between 12 and 24 hours, and the calendar flips right-to-left for Hebrew or Arabic. Every value comes straight from your browser; the code panel at the bottom shows the real return values.

What it is and why it matters

Intl.Locale has existed for years, but it only told you what was in a tag: language, script, region. The Intl Locale Info proposal adds methods that answer questions about a locale, using Unicode's locale data:

  • getWeekInfo(): firstDay (1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday) and weekend, an array of day numbers.
  • getHourCycles(): the preferred hour cycles, like ["h12"] for en-US or ["h23"] for ja-JP.
  • getTextInfo(): { direction: "ltr" } or "rtl".
  • getCalendars(): calendars in use, sorted by preference.
  • getTimeZones(): IANA time zones for the locale's region.

There are also getCollations() and getNumberingSystems(). The proposal reached Stage 4 and is part of ECMA-402, 13th edition (June 2026).

Why it matters: "the week starts on Sunday" is wrong for Spain, "the weekend is Saturday and Sunday" is wrong for Israel, and "use a 12-hour clock" is wrong for most of Europe. Before this, you either shipped a lookup table, pulled in a date library mainly for this, or guessed.

How it works

This is the core of the demo's calendar header. firstDay uses ISO numbering, so I build the seven column labels starting from it and let Intl.DateTimeFormat name each day:

const loc = new Intl.Locale(navigator.language);
const { firstDay, weekend } = loc.getWeekInfo();

const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(loc.baseName, { weekday: 'short', timeZone: 'UTC' });
const header = Array.from({ length: 7 }, (_, i) => {
  const isoDay = ((firstDay - 1 + i) % 7) + 1; // 1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday
  return fmt.format(new Date(Date.UTC(2024, 0, isoDay))); // 1 Jan 2024 was a Monday
});
// en-US → ["Sun", "Mon", …]   es-ES → ["lun", "mar", …]

A day is part of the weekend when weekend.includes(isoDay), which is how the demo paints the teal columns. Note that getDay() returns 0 for Sunday, so I convert with date.getDay() || 7.

For the clock, I take the first preferred hour cycle and pass it to DateTimeFormat. Intl.DateTimeFormat already picks a sensible default when formatting, so where this really pays off is in your own UI: choosing whether a time picker opens in 12 or 24 hours.

const [hourCycle] = loc.getHourCycles();
new Intl.DateTimeFormat(loc.baseName, { hour: 'numeric', minute: '2-digit', hourCycle });
// en-US → "6:05 PM"   es-ES → "18:05"

And getTextInfo().direction is what the demo uses to set dir="rtl" on the calendar.

The forced-region select in the demo uses the rg extension of the tag: en-US-u-rg-gbzzzz means "American English, but with UK regional preferences". Same language, but the week starts on Monday and the clock goes to 24 hours. That is a nice way to respect people who use a browser in English while living somewhere else.

I ran all of these snippets in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit through Playwright, and they returned the same week data in all three.

Browser support and gotchas

According to MDN's compatibility data, the methods shipped in Chrome 130, Safari 17 and, last, Firefox 153, which is what made the feature Baseline in July 2026. Node.js has the methods from version 24.

Things that will bite you:

  • The old accessor shape. Before the methods, Chrome (from 99), Safari (from 15.4) and Node (from 18) exposed these as properties (loc.weekInfo, loc.hourCycles…). They changed to methods because each access returned a new object, so loc.weekInfo === loc.weekInfo was false. If you need older engines, fall back: loc.getWeekInfo?.() ?? loc.weekInfo ?? { firstDay: 1, weekend: [6, 7] }. The demo does exactly that and shows a notice when it has to.
  • minimalDays is gone. Old docs show a third property for week-of-year rules. It has been removed from the spec and is being removed from browsers; none of the three engines I tested return it.
  • No region, no time zones. new Intl.Locale("es").getWeekInfo() still works, but getTimeZones() returns undefined when the tag has no region subtag. Try typing ar in the demo. Check before you call .length.
  • It is data, not a constant. The values come from Unicode locale data, and engines don't always agree on the long tail: for he-IL, Chromium and WebKit list islamic among the calendars and Firefox doesn't. Don't write tests that hardcode the full arrays.
  • navigator.language is a guess. It is the browser's UI language, not where the person lives. Let users override the first day of the week in settings; use this as the default.

What to keep an eye on

  • Date pickers and calendar components dropping their own week tables in favor of getWeekInfo().
  • Temporal, which pairs naturally with this for date maths once you know where the week starts.
  • How engines keep their locale data in sync, since small differences like the calendar list above can show up in UI.

Sources

  • Intl.Locale.prototype.getWeekInfo() – MDN
  • Intl.Locale.prototype.getHourCycles() – MDN
  • Intl.Locale.prototype.getTimeZones() – MDN
  • ECMA-402, 13th edition (June 2026)
  • Intl.Locale info – Web Platform Status

Originally published at richi.codes.

articles.title: Building a mortgage calculator that matches the CFPB's numbers to the cent
articles.description: Integer-cent arithmetic, a self-test contract every calculator must satisfy, and the 78%/80% PMI rule most tools get wrong.
articles.body_html:
Building a mortgage calculator that matches the CFPB's numbers to the cent

Every mortgage calculator I tried disagreed with the others by a few dollars. For a tool people use to decide a 30-year commitment, "close enough" is not a good answer. So I built one that does integer-cent arithmetic, prints every month of the schedule, and refuses to run if its own test cases fail.

Here is what actually mattered.

The formula is the easy part

The standard amortization payment is

P = L * i / (1 - (1 + i)^-n)

where L is the loan, i the monthly rate, n the number of payments. Anyone can type that. The disagreements come from everything around it.

Floating point is a bug in a money tool

If you compute 1234.56 * 360 in doubles and round at the end, you can land a cent off in a table of 360 rows, and users notice — they compare row 240 against their servicer's statement.

My rule: convert to integer cents at the input boundary, do all arithmetic in integers, divide only when rendering. Rate math is the one place where fractional arithmetic is unavoidable, so the monthly rate is computed once as rate / 100 / 12 and every intermediate money value is rounded to an integer cent at the row level, not at the end.

const toCents = (dollars) => Math.round(dollars * 100);
const pmt = (loanCents, monthlyRate, n) => {
  if (monthlyRate === 0) return Math.round(loanCents / n);
  const f = Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, -n);
  return Math.round((loanCents * monthlyRate) / (1 - f));
};

The monthlyRate === 0 branch is not theoretical: a 0% promo or an input of 0 used to produce NaN and a blank panel.

Rounding up is a product decision, not a detail

Payoff calculators have to decide what to do with a fractional final payment. I round up: if the amortization needs 48.3 payments, the answer is month 49, because that is the month the balance actually reaches zero in a servicer's ledger. Rounding down understates the term, which is the direction that misleads.

The test suite is the feature

Each calculator exposes the same shape:

window.CALC = { calc, cases, selfTest };

cases are inputs with expected outputs — including the ugly ones: zero price, 100% down payment, 1e309, a one-megabyte paste, an empty form. selfTest runs them in the page and returns a pass/fail array. A gate on my side loads the same file in node:vm and compares against an independent reimplementation, so the browser and the build agree.

That is also how I caught a real bug: a field declared min: 1 let someone enter a $1 house and produced "$5,000 in closing costs". The fix was a $10,000 floor, consistent with every other price field.

Two numbers people misread: 78% and 80%

PMI ends on two different triggers, and they are not the same date:

  • 78% of the home's original value, on the original amortization schedule — the servicer must terminate it, you do not have to ask.
  • 80% — you can request cancellation in writing, with conditions.

On a $360,000 loan at 6.5% with nothing down, those land at month 156 and month 146. Ten months of $165 premiums is $1,650 you get back by asking. The subtle part: extra principal moves your request date, not the statutory termination date, because the latter is defined against the original schedule.

What I deliberately left out

No framework, no build step, no npm install: one stylesheet, one small core.js, one file per calculator. The whole site is static, ~140 KB on the heaviest page, and every calculator works with JavaScript enabled and no network after load. No numbers are uploaded — there is no endpoint to upload to.

Ads are the funding model, and the honest part of that is layout: an ad above the form pushes the form off a phone screen, so the ad unit sits below the calculator, and an unfilled unit collapses to zero height instead of leaving a 280px hole.

Try it and tell me where it is wrong

The calculators, the assumptions, and the citation list are all public: mujingame.xin. If a number disagrees with your servicer's statement, the methodology page says exactly which convention is used, so the disagreement is checkable instead of a matter of trust.

If you are building something similar, the two things I would copy are the integer-cent boundary and the self-test contract. Everything else is style.

articles.title: The numbers behind a one-button wall jump
articles.description: We made a small browser game called Wall Jump Tower. You press one button. Your climber jumps from...
articles.body_html:
We made a small browser game called Wall Jump Tower. You press one button. Your climber jumps from one wall to the
other while lava rises under you. It runs in the browser with no sign-up:
https://thumbyard.com/go/wjt-devto

With one button there is nothing to hide behind. If the jump feels a little off, the player has no other input to
blame, so the jump is the whole game. Before we tuned anything we studied
Celeste, Super Meat Boy, N++, Mega Man X and Hollow Knight, and wrote down every constant we could trace to a source.
This post is what we kept, with our real values.

Gravity is three numbers, not one

Our climber launches at 610 px/s. Gravity depends on what the player is doing:

p.vy += (p.vy > 0 ? 2000 : inp.hold && p.vy > -90 ? 800 : 1500) * dt;
if (p.vy > 900) p.vy = 900;
  • Rising: 1500 px/s^2.
  • Falling: 2000 px/s^2. A heavier fall makes the arc feel snappy instead of floaty.
  • Near the top of the arc while the button is held: 800. That gives a short hang where you can read the next wall. Celeste does the same thing with its HalfGravThreshold (half gravity while jump is held and vertical speed is under 40 px/s).
  • Fall speed caps at 900 px/s, so a long drop stays readable on a phone screen.

Physics at a fixed 120 steps a second

If physics steps once per drawn frame, a 60 Hz laptop and a 120 Hz phone give different jumps for the same
tap, and a one-button game cannot afford that. Our physics runs at a fixed 1/120 s step from an accumulator, whatever
the screen does. A run is just the list of steps where the button went down, so it replays the same on any screen.
That is what makes the ghost of your best run, and challenge links to a friend, possible.

A 0.14 s grip before the wall slide

When the climber touches a wall in the air it sticks for 0.14 s before it starts to slide (slides cap at 70 px/s).
Without the grip, a tap that lands a hair late finds the climber already sliding away and the kick looks weak. With it,
late taps still feel like clean kicks. Ice walls skip the grip on purpose.

Small helpers the player never sees

  • Corner correction: if the head clips the corner of a ledge by a few pixels on the way up, we nudge the climber sideways instead of killing the jump.
  • Ledge pull-up: a jump that ends with the feet just under a ledge lifts onto it.
  • The lava waits for your first press, so reading the level is free.

When a one-button puzzle feels pixel perfect

Level 9 has two circles that throw you upward. A playtester got stuck there and said it felt pixel perfect. We measured
the tap window with a script that tries every press time: the first circle gave an average of 113 ms. The fix did not
touch the jump numbers. A held press now fires a circle as you pass through it, and a press just before a circle waits
for it instead of spending your air jump. The window went to 182 ms, and one held press from the floor now carries
through both circles.

Animation follows physics, never the other way

Every clip is timed in milliseconds, not display frames, so 60 Hz and 120 Hz look the same. A turn takes 100 ms, as in
Hollow Knight, and a wall kick 167 ms (four frames at Hollow Knight's 24 fps wall-jump rate), and no animation ever delays a jump: physics decides,
the sprite catches up.

That is most of it. The game has 15 short levels, and every level keeps a ghost of your best
run. If you try it, we would like to know which level stopped you first:
https://thumbyard.com/go/wjt-devto

articles.title: Why PDF form answers vanish: field values, appearance streams and flattening in pdf-lib
articles.description: A complaint that turns up on every PDF help forum: "I filled in the form, sent it, and they say it's...
articles.body_html:
A complaint that turns up on every PDF help forum: "I filled in the form, sent it, and they say it's blank." Both people are usually telling the truth. The answers are in the file, and the recipient's viewer is not drawing them.

If you generate or fill PDF forms in code, this is worth understanding properly, because the same mechanism causes the "I saved it and my answers are gone" reports, and the fix in code is a few lines once you know where the data lives.

A field stores its answer twice

An AcroForm text field is a dictionary in the file, and the thing you see on the page is a widget annotation attached to it. The two parts that matter here:

  • /V on the field is the value: the string the person typed.
  • /AP on the widget is the appearance: a small content stream, a Form XObject, that draws the box and the text inside it.

A viewer showing a form normally paints /AP, not /V. The value is data. The appearance is the picture of the data. When the two disagree, what you see depends on whether the viewer trusts the picture or rebuilds it from the value.

So there are three ways a filled form ends up showing nothing:

  1. The value never reached the file. The person typed into a browser's built-in viewer, which held the values in memory, then downloaded the original instead of the edited copy, or closed the tab.
  2. The value is there, the picture is stale. Some filling code writes /V and never regenerates /AP. A viewer that paints the stored appearance shows the empty box it was created with.
  3. The form is XFA. The real form is an XML payload inside the PDF, and the page content is a placeholder telling you to open it in Adobe Reader. Viewers that do not run XFA have nowhere to put your typing.

There is a fourth, older variant: forms created for free Adobe Reader under "Reader Extensions" usage rights, which for years could be filled but not saved unless the author had enabled the document. Modern readers mostly ignore this, but old templates still carry the flags.

Reproducing case two

Case two is the one code causes, so it is the one worth seeing. Here is a field with a value and a stale appearance, built with pdf-lib:

import { PDFDocument, PDFName, PDFString } from 'pdf-lib';

const doc = await PDFDocument.create();
const page = doc.addPage([400, 200]);
const field = doc.getForm().createTextField('name');
field.addToPage(page, { x: 50, y: 100, width: 200, height: 24 }); // creates an empty appearance

// Write the value directly, the way a careless filler would
field.acroField.dict.set(PDFName.of('V'), PDFString.of('Ada Lovelace'));
const bytes = await doc.save({ updateFieldAppearances: false });

Open that file in a viewer that paints stored appearances and the box is empty, while any tool that reads /V reports "Ada Lovelace". I checked it with PyMuPDF: get_text() on the page returns an empty string, because the value is not page content and the appearance has nothing in it.

Two details there are worth knowing:

  • save() in pdf-lib defaults to updateFieldAppearances: true, and setText() marks the field so its appearance is rebuilt. If you go through the high-level API you are mostly safe. Writing /V by hand, or copying values between documents at the dictionary level, is how stale appearances get made.
  • Checking that /AP exists does not prove anything. The widget above has an appearance. It is just the wrong one.

The old escape hatch: /NeedAppearances

The AcroForm dictionary can carry /NeedAppearances true, which asks the viewer to regenerate every appearance from the values on open. Many fillers set it instead of drawing appearances themselves. It helps in viewers that honour it, and does nothing in viewers that do not, and PDF 2.0 deprecates it. Treat it as a hint, not a fix.

The fix that works everywhere: flatten a copy

Flattening draws each widget's appearance into the page content and removes the fields. After that, the answers are ordinary page content, the same as printed text, and no viewer can fail to show them. The form stops being a form, so flatten a copy you are sending and keep the fillable original.

import { PDFDocument, PDFName, PDFTextField } from 'pdf-lib';

export async function flattenForSending(bytes) {
  const doc = await PDFDocument.load(bytes);
  const form = doc.getForm();
  if (form.hasXFA()) form.deleteXFA(); // drop the XML form; the AcroForm fields remain

  // Rebuild every text field's appearance from its value, then draw it into the page.
  for (const field of form.getFields()) {
    if (field instanceof PDFTextField) field.setText(field.getText());
  }
  form.flatten();

  // flatten() removes the widgets but can leave their references in /Annots.
  for (const page of doc.getPages()) {
    const annots = page.node.Annots();
    if (!annots) continue;
    const live = annots.asArray().filter((ref) => doc.context.lookup(ref) !== undefined);
    page.node.set(PDFName.of('Annots'), doc.context.obj(live));
  }
  return doc.save();
}

Run on the broken file above, the result has no widgets and the page text reads "Ada Lovelace".

Three things in that function cost me time:

  • instanceof, not constructor.name. My first version checked field.constructor.name === 'PDFTextField'. Against the minified build the class names are mangled, the check never matched, nothing was rebuilt, and flatten faithfully drew the empty appearance into the page. The output looked flattened and was blank.
  • The dangling references. With the pdf-lib build I used, flatten() deleted the widget objects but left 7 0 R in the page's /Annots array. The spec says a reference to a missing object is treated as null, so most viewers cope, but MuPDF printed "cannot find object in xref" on every open, and strict validators are less forgiving. The cleanup loop removes the dead references.
  • XFA. deleteXFA() removes the XML form, and the AcroForm fields that were generated alongside it stay. For a static XFA form that is usually what you want. For a dynamic XFA form there may be no useful AcroForm underneath, and the only fix is asking the issuer for a regular PDF.

For the people filling the form

All of this is invisible to the person who just wants their answers to arrive. The advice for them is short: download the blank form before typing, fill it in a desktop reader or a tool that writes the file, and flatten the copy you send. I point people to a reader-friendly guide to PDF form fields that won't save, which matches each symptom to its cause without any of the dictionary talk.

For the people writing the code: never write /V without rebuilding /AP, and if the output is going to someone else, flatten it.

articles.title: I built a Wordle-style math game in a single HTML file that has turned into a daily morning rivalry with my dad and daughter
articles.description: In 2022, right when everyone was obsessed with Wordle, I paid a freelance developer on Fiverr to...
articles.body_html:
In 2022, right when everyone was obsessed with Wordle, I paid a freelance developer on Fiverr to build a simple idea I had in my head: a 60-second daily mental math game.

They built what I asked for. It worked fine. And nobody played it, including me.

It just felt clunky, like a digital worksheet. So I closed the folder and left it sitting on my hard drive for four years.

A few weeks ago I dug the idea back up. I wanted a quick numbers game that my dad, my daughter, and I could play every morning the same way we play Wordle. So I threw out the 2022 code and rebuilt Mathing from scratch in a single HTML file.

No frameworks, no sign-ups, no ads. Just a 60-second timer. Now it's a daily morning rivalry in our family group chat.

If you want to see how fast you are before reading how it works, today's puzzle takes 60 seconds:
Play today's Mathing at mathing.co

(The average score across all players this week is 24. The highest score anyone has hit so far is 55. If you beat 30 on your first run, drop your score in the comments.)

Why most speed math games feel slow: the Enter key

When I tested early versions of the game, something felt off.

Suppose the screen shows 14 + 19 = ?. You know the answer is 33 almost immediately.
Still, your hand has to:

  1. Press 3
  2. Press 3
  3. Reach over and hit Enter (or tap a submit button on your phone)
  4. Wait for the next question to load

At that point you aren't testing mental math anymore. You're testing how fast your thumb can jump back and forth to the Enter key.

To fix that, I got rid of the Enter key completely.

The whole game is built around one constraint: every answer is a single digit from 0 to 9.

The problems themselves still use two-digit numbers (63 ÷ 9 = ?, 15 - 8 = ?, 7 × 1 = ?), so you still have to calculate. Because the answer is always a single digit (0-9), the moment you press a number key, it submits and the next problem appears immediately.

No Enter key, no backspace, and no multi-digit typing. Once you get into a rhythm, the game moves as fast as you can read.

The 0ms transition problem

Once you remove the Enter key, people play much faster, and normal UI animations start getting in the way.

In my first build, tapping an answer flashed the box green or red for 250ms before showing the next equation.

That felt awful. If you answer 40 questions in a minute, a 250ms pause on each one eats up 10 full seconds of your 60-second timer.

On the other hand, when I made the next problem appear in 0ms with no animation at all, it was jarring. If two problems in a row looked similar, you couldn't tell if your tap had registered.

I ended up splitting the answer box into two layers:

  • The actual equation updates in 0ms, so your eyes can read the next problem right away.
  • A separate overlay (#answer-ghost) flashes the number you just pressed in green or red for 300ms on top of the box without blocking your next keypress. 
function showFeedback(correct, val) {
  elAnswerGhost.className = 'eq-answer-ghost';
  elAnswerGhost.textContent = val;
  void elAnswerGhost.offsetWidth; // Restart CSS animation on rapid keypresses
  elAnswerGhost.className = 'eq-answer-ghost ' + (correct ? 'ghost-correct' : 'ghost-wrong');
}

Forcing a reflow with void elAnswerGhost.offsetWidth; lets the green/red flash restart cleanly even when someone is answering two questions a second.

Giving everyone the same daily questions without a backend

For a family rivalry to be fair, a score of 38 on my phone has to mean the exact same thing as a 38 on my dad's phone. If one person gets easy addition and someone else gets division, the scores don't mean anything.

Instead of running a backend database to serve daily puzzles, the game uses a 25-line seeded random number generator in the browser, seeded by the local date (YYYY-MM-DD):

function SeededRandom(seed) {
  this.m = 0x80000000;
  this.a = 1103515245;
  this.c = 12345;
  this.state = seed ? seed : Math.floor(Math.random() * (this.m - 1));
}

At midnight, the date string hashes into a seed and generates a sequence of 300 problems. Everyone playing today's Daily mode gets the exact same problems in the exact same order.

Plugging the loopholes players found this week

Earlier this week, a player named Adam emailed me a few loopholes he found after playing a couple of rounds (he scored 34, then 41):

  1. Quitting mid-round to retry: If you messed up the first 10 seconds of the Daily puzzle, you could tap Home (or refresh the page) before time ran out and start the Daily over, having already seen the first 15 questions.
  2. UTC vs. local midnight: new Date('2026-10-01') parses as UTC midnight in JavaScript, while new Date(2026, 9, 1) uses local time. Because of that, the puzzle number (#47 -> #48) was flipping at 7:00 PM EST, five hours before the actual questions reset at local midnight.

I pushed fixes for both last night. Today's daily run now locks as soon as the timer starts, and the puzzle number rolls over at local midnight right alongside the question seed.

Give today's puzzle a shot

If you have 60 seconds to spare, try today's daily round here: https://www.mathing.co/

Here is where the numbers sit over the past 7 days:

  • Average daily score: 24.2 solved
  • Current high score: 55 solved (95% accuracy)

If you play a round, click Share at the end and paste your score in the comments.
